metadata.title: What is a buying group?
metadata.author: Marketing Business Network
metadata.shortDescription:
A buying group combines the purchasing requirements of separate buyers. Follow three independent cafes that each need one thousand identical paper cups.

See how the combined requirement reaches three thousand cups, why better terms are possible rather than guaranteed, and how costs, commitments and independent ownership fit together.

Thank you for watching. Like this video and subscribe to Marketing Business Network for clear business and marketing explainers.

Sources:
https://www.accc.gov.au/system/files/supermarkets-inquiry_1.pdf
https://www.accc.gov.au/system/files/public-registers/documents/MER16%2B8455.pdf
https://about.openfoodnetwork.org.au/project/consumer-buying-groups/

segments.text: What is a buying group?
A buying group brings separate buyers together to purchase goods or
services on agreed terms.
By combining their demand, members may be able to negotiate better prices
or other benefits than they could obtain alone.
Buying groups can take different forms.
In business, members often keep running their own companies while
cooperating on purchasing.
Imagine three independent cafes that use the same plain paper cups.
Each needs one thousand cups for its next order.
On its own, each cafe approaches the supplier with an order for one
thousand.
Together, the cafes can discuss a combined requirement of three thousand
cups.
The product has not changed.
The quantity being negotiated has.
The group first needs to agree what it wants: the cup size, quality,
quantities and delivery requirements.
Its organizer can then ask suppliers for terms based on that shared demand.
Depending on the arrangement, members might order directly from the selected
supplier, or the group might arrange a combined purchase and distribution.
The actual ordering system matters.
A supplier may offer a lower unit price, more useful payment terms or
a better delivery arrangement.
That is a possibility, not a guaranteed result.
The supplier still has production, delivery and administrative costs.
Members should compare the complete offer, including transport and any group
fees, rather than assume that a larger order is automatically the cheapest
option.
Cooperation also brings practical decisions.
One cafe might want different cups, another might need an urgent delivery
and a third might not have room to store a large order.
Minimum commitments or membership fees may apply.
A useful buying group has rules for these differences, and members need to
understand what they are agreeing to before joining.
Joining a buying group does not necessarily mean that the cafes merge or
become one chain.
They can remain separately owned businesses, with their own customers and
operations.
Also, agreeing purchasing terms is different from agreeing what each cafe
will charge its customers.
Cooperation between competitors needs to stay within the competition rules
that apply to the arrangement.
For our cafes, the buying group changes the supplier conversation from three
separate small requirements to one coordinated larger requirement.
Whether it is worthwhile depends on the real terms, costs and obligations.
The core idea is simple: buyers combine purchasing power while deciding
carefully which parts of the purchase to organize together.
Thank you for watching.
If this helped, please like the video and subscribe to Marketing Business
Network for more clear business explainers.

metadata.title: I Investigated Ticket Scalping (it's worse than I thought)
metadata.author: Ben Farr
metadata.shortDescription:
Over the last few years, it feels like it's been harder and harder to get tickets to concerts and events. I always thought that this was because more people wanted to go. But it turns out a big piece of it comes down to scalpers - professional resellers who use bots, tools, and tricks to claim all the tickets before fans even get a chance.

✉ Learn to grow your own YouTube channel!
https://bit.ly/benfarr-newsletter

Hit me up, let's chat! 👇
📷 Instagram: https://instagram.com/benfarr.yt
🦉 Twitter: https://twitter.com/benfarryt

🔔 Subscribe to get my latest uploads first!
https://www.youtube.com/bxnsfilms?sub_confirmation=1

🧠 About Me
Hey, I'm Ben! I've always been naturally curious, looking at the world around me and trying to figure out how it works. On this channel, I set out to learn about trends, culture, and the everyday life we all live - to equip you with a deep understanding of our wonderful world.

📚 Video Chapters
0:00 I Was Wrong About Tickets...
0:40 The Situation
1:50 How Scalping works
3:12 Going Undercover
5:04 How Ticketmaster works
6:49 The Toolkit
8:28 The Problem
11:33 Why no one is fixing this
12:44 Ticketmaster's secret
14:04 Soooo.... regulations?
15:24 What can you do?
16:39 One More Thing...

metadata.title: How Ticketmaster Makes Money From Tickets It Already Sold (Taylor Swift Fans Know)
metadata.author: Cash Dissected
metadata.shortDescription:
A fan listed her Bruno Mars ticket for $299. She would get $254.15. The buyer would pay $422.45. Same seat, same show, and Ticketmaster in the middle of both sides.

In this video, we follow one $70 concert ticket from checkout to resale to the parking lot, and count every time Ticketmaster and its owner, Live Nation, get paid along the way.

You'll learn:
- Where all those fees at checkout actually go
- How one company ended up running the ticket line for almost every big stage in America
- How Ticketmaster gets paid again when you resell a ticket
- What Live Nation employees said about fans in Slack messages shown at trial
- What the FTC says about brokers, bots and $3.7 billion in resale fees
- Why the ticket business makes more profit than the concerts themselves
- What the April 2026 monopoly verdict means for ticket prices
- How to pay less in fees right now

The concerts are the show. The tickets are the business.

This video is for education and entertainment only and is not financial or legal advice. The FTC lawsuit contains allegations, not a ruling. Live Nation disputes them and is fighting the jury verdict.

Maya's $70 ticket is an example. The fee estimate uses the ~35% average from the New York ticket fee study.

#Ticketmaster #LiveNation #TaylorSwift #ErasTour #ConcertTickets #TicketFees #HiddenFees #Monopoly #FTC #MoneyExplained #HowCompaniesMakeMoney #BusinessExplained #BusinessModel #Economics

metadata.title: Buying the Float: The Hidden Cash Flow Trap in Every Deal
metadata.author: Walker Deibel
metadata.shortDescription:
Most buyers underwrite profit and forget the one thing that will quietly bleed them dry: _the float._

It’s the gap between when you pay your vendors and when your customers pay you. Ignore it, and you can bleed six figures of cash in your first year—even if the business looks profitable on paper.

This video is _Part 2 of my 3-part Cash Flow Series_. In Part 1, we looked at the clash of the two clocks. In this video, we’re tackling the float. 

In this video, I’ll show you:

- How to measure working capital in real dollars (DSO, DPO, DIO)
- Why terms matter more than sales in your first year of ownership
- How to build the float into your deal so *you’re not the bank*
- A pro tip to unlock an extra 10 days of cash within 90 days of closing

Sales won’t kill you. _Terms will._ If you want your deal to survive post-close, you need to know how to underwrite the float.

*📌 Want to go deeper?*

💼 Learn how to buy a business in 6–12 months at https://bit.ly/3HYI08d
📩 Get insights like this in your inbox: https://bit.ly/4oXpCgx
📚 Grab the bestselling book: https://www.amazon.com/Buy-Then-Build-Acquisition-Entrepreneurs/dp/1544501137/

👍 Like this video? Drop a comment below with your biggest takeaway or question!

#AcquisitionEntrepreneurship #BuyThenBuild #BusinessAcquisition #Entrepreneurship #SmallBusinessOwner

segments.text: Most people don't realize this, but you
might qualify for a business credit card
and not even know it. Any kind of
freelance work or side hustle, even if
that's Uber or Door Dash, all unlock the
world of business credit cards, which
means higher welcome offers and
additional perks. And perhaps the best
premium option in this category is the
Capital 1 Venture X Business. So, let's
go over the core features of this
frequently overlooked card and help you
determine whether or not you're eligible
and if this is a product worth adding to
your wallet.
[Music]
Let's start with the basics, including
who is eligible for business credit
cards. And if you do want to learn more
about the Venture X business or any of
our other favorite business credit
cards, then be sure to check out the
links down in the description since they
also help us make more of these free
videos, which we really appreciate. So,
first, the bad news. The Venture X
business does come with an annual fee of
which certainly isn't cheap, but for a
premium business card, it's actually
reasonable. And as you'll see in a
minute, it is one of the easiest credit
cards to justify in terms of the annual
fee. But the big headline is the welcome
offer. 150,000 Capital 1 miles after
spending $30,000 in the first 3 months.
And let's just say the quiet part out
loud. That spending requirement is
steep, especially if you're used to
personal cards. So, you'll definitely
need some substantial and legitimate
business expenses in order to earn that
welcome offer. And I'll tell you about
my secret way to hit those high spending
requirements on business cards in a
minute. But even outside the welcome
offer, the Venture X business still has
a lot to offer. First up, you get a $300
annual travel credit when booking
through Capital 1 Travel, which is the
main reason I say this is the easiest
premium card to justify since even if
you only take one trip per year, that's
going to knock down your effective
annual fee to just 95 bucks. Then, every
card anniversary, you get 10,000 bonus
miles, which are worth around a hundred
bucks minimum, even at 1 cent per point.
So, we're only two benefits in and we've
already completely covered the annual
fee. But you'll also get unlimited
lounge access, including Capital 1 and
Priority Pass lounges. And lastly, you
can fly through security with a $120
credit towards TSA PreCheck or Global
Entry. And remember that Pre-Check comes
with Global Entry. So, if you're going
to go through the whole sign up process,
then I always recommend that you just go
ahead and get Global Entry since again
it comes with TSA PreCheck. It's also
worth noting that there are a few
business specific differences between
this card and the very popular personal
Venture X, like the fact that this is a
charge card with no preset spending
limit. So, it adapts to your business
spending and also requires you to pay
off the balance in full at the end of
each month, which personally I'm a huge
fan of since you should always be doing
that anyway. Similar to adding
authorized users to a personal card,
with the Venture X business, you can add
employee cards for free, and they offer
tools to manage their spending and track
all those business expenses. Speaking of
spending, the Venture X business keeps
it pretty simple in terms of the
spending multipliers. You'll earn 2
miles per dollar on every purchase with
no limits or categories to keep track
of. And if you use the Capital 1 travel
portal, which you can learn more about
in this video, you'll earn 10 m per
dollar on hotels and rental cars on top
of the 5 miles you'll earn on flights
and vacation rentals. So, booking your
business travel through Capital 1 Travel
will have you raking in those Capital 1
miles. Now, one last bonus tip for you.
If you also hold a cashback card like
the Capital 1 Spark Cash, you can
actually convert that cash back into
miles with your Venture X business,
making this an incredible twocard setup.
Okay, so the Venture X business
obviously offers a lot of value. But who
is this right for and who should look
elsewhere? Well, for frequent business
travelers, this card is an obvious
choice. If you're flying often or even
just a few times per year and you want
lounge access, travel credits, and
better earning on flights and hotels,
then this card will more than pay for
itself. It's also a great choice for
high spend business owners since the
simple 2x on everything with no spending
limit means you'll be raking in Capital
1 miles. Again, just keep in mind that
being a charge card means that you do
have to pay it off in full every single
month, which again I'm a huge fan of.
And lastly, if you've already got
something like the Spark Cash card, then
pairing it with the Venture X business
unlocks the cash back to miles
conversion that we just talked about.
And again, I remind you when I say
business owners, I'm not just talking
about big multi-million dollar
companies. Any kind of side hustle, sole
proprietorship, or 1099 freelance work
of any kind is a business and should be
treated as such, meaning you're
separating your personal and business
expenses. Otherwise, things can get a
little dicey come tax season. So, if you
fall into any of those categories, then
everything I just said also applies to
you. That does, however, bring us to who
should probably go with a different
business card. Obviously, if you don't
have a business or don't travel at all
for business, then you're not going to
get the value out of the travel credits
or lounge perks. Additionally, if you're
a very low spend business, then the 30k
spend requirement for the welcome offer
is probably out of reach. Now, you can
get creative with this by timing any
large upcoming expenses. Or do what I do
and put your quarterly taxes on your
business credit card in order to meet
the higher spending requirements. But
without fairly substantial profits, even
that strategy is not going to get you
anywhere close to that $30,000
requirement for the Venture X business.
So, do the napkin math and see if it's
feasible for you because there's plenty
of other great options out there with
lower spending requirements. And the
last thing I want you to do is go out
and needlessly spend money on things
that you wouldn't otherwise be buying
just for the sake of earning a welcome
offer because I promise the math does
not math on that one. But even outside
of that welcome offer, I think this card
is a worthwhile addition to even the
most casual business traveler's wallet
and will more than pay for itself given
the easy to use benefits it offers.
Again, if you want to learn more about
the Capital 1 Venture X business and
help support this free content, then be
sure to check out that first link down
in the description since using that link
doesn't cost you anything, but it does
help support Daily Drop, which we really
appreciate. Let us know what you think
of this product down in the comment
section. And as always, thank you so
much for watching, and we'll see you in
the next video. Here we go.

That does, however, bring us to who should probably go with a different business card. metadata.shortDescription:
Wondering what it's like to have NBA season tickets? I've had season tickets for 4 NBA seasons for the Denver Nuggets, and in this video, I share what it's like to go to games, manage and sell your tickets, how much it really costs, and all the perks of being an NBA season ticket member. 

Everyone knows that season tickets aren't cheap, and with 41 home games during the NBA regular season, it can be a lot to manage. From a season ticket holder's perspective, I'll give you some tips on how to decide if season tickets are right for you, and share some things that I've learned along the way after having both NBA and NFL season tickets in Denver and LA. 

If you're thinking about getting tickets to sell because you're wondering how much money you can make off of them, I'll also share a lot about the selling process that you might not know or think about as an NBA fan interested in selling some tickets.

that they should sit for their season tickets and while it does depend I do have some advice for you if you're going to go to a lot of games you should like where you sit and I always recommend to people to get a smaller ticket package maybe something like a 10 game weekend package or a half season package before you commit to a full season of NBA games because you really want to know that the place that you're committing to is a good spot for you for me I said in the last row of the 100 level semi-diagonal to the hoop this picture right here is actually the exact view from my seats at ball Arena and I'll tell you why I like these tickets a lot I think being in the back section of the 100 level is actually a very good value seat before seats start getting really expensive but you know if metadata.title: How NBA Season Tickets Actually Work (From a 7-Year Holder)
metadata.author: Dave Chung
metadata.shortDescription:
Is buying NBA season tickets a dream for basketball fans or a financial and logistical nightmare? After 7 years as a Denver Nuggets season ticket holder, I’m breaking down the real costs, the hidden perks, and the things your ticket rep won't tell you.

🚀 Manage your tickets easily with TiqAssist: https://www.tiqassist.com?grsf=davechung
(I’ve used them for years to automate my resale and they are a lifesaver for busy people!)

0:00 Intro
0:10 Do you get playoff tickets?
0:47 How playoff ticket payments work
1:26 Are playoff tickets included?
1:53 Are prices locked in?
2:09 How much do playoff tickets cost?
3:12 How regular season payments work
3:47 Same seats for the whole season?
4:11 If you have bad seat neighbors
5:00 Where to get season tickets
5:23 How to try before you buy
6:00 Trading tickets for other sections
6:23 How to bring more people to games
6:34 Easy way to buy and sell tickets
7:54 Member-exclusive swag and experiences
8:34 Access to preseason scrimmage
9:15 Events the Nuggets have every year
10:24 Help others learn how this works
10:44 How things have changed
10:58 Member-only social events
11:57 Regular season unique perks
13:52 Teams should give this to season ticket members
14:20 Season tickets and NBA League Pass
14:51 Better seats, better perks?
15:17 How to take advantage of perks
15:43 Once-in-a-lifetime events
16:38 Section-specific benefits
17:21 Can you switch seats mid-season?
17:38 How to relocate your seats for next season
18:30 Why I left the 100 level
19:10 The best NBA experience I've ever had



Whether you are looking at your first pair of tickets or you’ve been a member for years, this video covers the logistics that every NBA fan needs to know. We dive into the "Pay as You Play" playoff model, how to handle the seat relocation window, and why your "neighbors" matter just as much as your view of the court.

I also share my strategy for managing the 41-game grind, including how I automate my ticket resale to ensure my seats never go to waste when I can't make a game.

In this video, we discuss:
- How playoff billing actually works (and why it’s "pay as they play").
- The 300% price increase I’ve seen over 7 years.
- Why I moved seats because of "bad neighbors."
- The best "value" sections for resale and viewing.
- Season Ticket Member (STM) perks: From high-fives to League Pass.
- How to handle the "frantic" seat relocation window.

But, even now that the team is popular events have kind of become less exclusive, I can bank on a few events a year. Pretty [music] much every December, season ticket members get to play on the court while the Nuggets are on a long road trip. This actually used to be small enough that we could play a giant game of knockout, where I came in third, I believe, 2 years in a row. But, it's just way too big to do that. Now that there are so many more season ticket members, there are just balls flying everywhere, and kids pretty much get hit in the head nonstop. And it's still fun, but it's honestly a little bit more fun for teenagers and grown-ups because we can kind of protect ourselves from all the air balls from adults who haven't shot a basketball in decades. This year, they actually switched things up, and they played the Grinch on the jumbotron, which was great for younger kids and just families who are coming there to hang out. Younger kids could just sit and watch a movie instead of going on the court and getting hit directly in the face with basketballs. For us, our kids love going to the arena even when there's not a game going on. They just kind of run around [music] in the seats and getting to watch a movie this year and hang out with Rocky made it even better. So, that's something really fun to do and it's a unique way to spend the afternoon during the winter time. If you're enjoying this video so far, please give it a like to help more people find it and especially if you live in Denver, feel free to subscribe. I make videos and shorts with things to do and places to eat every week in our city. If you have other questions I somehow miss in this video, feel free to add them to the comments. I'll try to reply like I've done before, but let's keep this thing moving. So, that preseason scrimmage that I mentioned, now it's opened up to general admission. It's kind of a bummer because that scrimmage felt really exclusive before, but really it's, you know, this is pre-preseason, so it's kind of the more the merrier. Let's all get hyped for the season. There's also kind of one silly event per year where they will put players on stage and have them do like a family feud type of thing or something similar to that. That's a season ticket member only event. It's a fun way to watch your players let loose, [music] but you don't get to like get autographs with them or take pictures with them like we could in the past. And I'm certainly not complaining. I know that some of you guys in larger markets or when your team is really good, get absolutely nothing. So, the fact that we do get some access to the team while our team is still good, that's still a great thing. Definitely not complaining [music] at all. But if you think you're going to meet the team, get pictures and autographs and all this swag, if you're in a big market or your team is good, you probably won't. You know, when the Nuggets weren't very good, that stuff was more accessible. You know, we took pictures with the players, there were smaller events, but, you know, if your team is bad and you're still a really big fan, this could be a great way to take advantage of it. I bet your perks are way better than some of the big market teams. In addition to these events, we also have an app where we can use credits in exchange for experiences or swag. On the swag side, it's usually things like bobbleheads and mystery bags of team gear. But what's cooler is those free or discounted experiences that we can use our credits for. Like this year, I used my credits [music] to get this Bruce Brown bobblehead that they gave away at a game that I didn't go to earlier in the season. I also got this model of Ball Arena, which you might think is stupid, but I think it's kind of cool because it shows the actual court inside and I can [music] see where we sit, which is kind of fun. I also had our 5-year-old give players a high-five on their way out to the court at a game earlier this season. If you have a kid who you are planning to bring to games with you sometime, definitely ask the season ticket rep if you have access to something like this because this can create some really special memories. I had to pay for this one, but I got two of my friends on the court to hold the American flag during the national anthem at a game earlier this season. It's really cool because you're standing directly on the court while players are actively warming up for about 10 minutes right before tip-off. It is one of the best things that you get as a season ticket member. It was even better when it was free, but for $100 a person, it's something that most of your friends have never done and they will never do again in their lifetime. [music] I can also use my credits to do things like watch warm-ups if I want to get to the game really early like if I'm catching up with a friend or a super fan. We also have a couple times a year where there's like a team alumnus. I think this year was Danilo Gallinari and Nene. You could use your credits to take a picture with them before the game. I also get 10% off regularly priced items at the team store at the stadium and online, but we all know that that's not that great of a deal because there's always a coupon code that you can get like 25% off of stuff throughout [music] the season, so it's there, but it doesn't matter that much. They always sell out in all of the normal people sizes. And getting access to those even 24 hours early, that would be great. Another thing that they've started giving to us is a free NBA League Pass subscription. I always hope that one day the local blackout restrictions won't happen and then that NBA League Pass subscription will be pretty awesome. A few years back when I was doing that American flag thing, I talked to a guy who has season tickets that are basically courtside. But for these experiences and things that take these credits, it can be a little tricky if you're splitting your season tickets with someone else because if they're the primary person on the account, you want to make sure that they're actually checking their email and they're keeping track of these things. It's also a lot less crowded on club level. I just think that we have more places to like sit [music] and hang out. So, if you are going to the game to catch up with friends or maybe you want to get there early to just make a whole night out of it, club level is really convenient and very comfortable for that. Some people have asked me about switching seats and at least for the Nuggets, you can't switch your seats partway through the season. I tried during that season where I had the people who are swearing and knew nothing about basketball, but I wasn't able to actually switch my seats that season, so I just kind of did it on my own by selling and buying. But every year there is a seat relocation window where you can add seats, move your seats, you can upgrade, downgrade, all of the stuff that you would expect. An important thing to know is that that relocation window is pretty insane. Like seats are coming and going as people are moving seats, adding seats to their carts, removing seats from their carts. I would highly recommend doing it from a computer instead of doing it on your phone like I did last year. It was super stressful. Like I really wanted to be in the front row in a corner section on the club level. It was very specific what I was going for, so [music] I was very frantic trying to find these seats and they weren't available until they were and I grabbed them and I checked out so fast, but if I was doing it on a computer, it would have been a lot less stressful. And I was on vacation, so I was doing it while we were on the road. I wasn't driving, but it was crazy. And the reason why we wanted these seats in particular is because our kids are five and two. If we were in our old seats, which was the last row of the 100 level, if there's an adult who sits in front of them, they basically can't see the entire time. When we're in the front row of a higher section, there's no one in front of them, so they can stand up, [music] they can walk around if they want, they can see the game and, you know, they're really bothering nobody versus kind of being squeezed into the regular section. You know, it's a lot of fun down on the 100 level, but it just [music] didn't work for our life stage anymore, so I wanted those tickets and I aggressively [music] got them. But even after seven years of having season tickets and watching our team win a championship, there is one NBA experience that I will never forget and that was sitting courtside. If you've ever wondered what it's like to sit in the front row at an NBA game, this video will show you everything there is to [music] know from start to finish and I'll catch you over there.

metadata.title: 7,624 tickets to one concert: the REPS ticket broker file
metadata.author: Sygnify Data
metadata.shortDescription:
A federal lawsuit filed on 15 October 2026 alleges that REPS & Company, a San Diego ticket broker, used at least 1,300 accounts to buy 7,624 tickets to one stadium concert in 2023, where the limit was four to eight a buyer. The complaint, filed by the Justice Department for the FTC, says that from January 2022 to October 2025 REPS bought more than eight tickets for at least 83,000 events: over 18.5 million tickets, for over $1.3 billion, and at least $120.8 million in resale profit. It describes accounts opened in employees' and partners' names under power of attorney agreements, small changes to an address after a "limit error", an internal "Error Bible", proxies, multi-session browsers and banks of SIM cards. The law in the case, the Better Online Ticket Sales Act, bars getting around the controls a ticket seller uses to enforce posted ticket limits. REPS says it never uses bots, that it uses real people with real accounts, and that it looks forward to presenting its case in court. No court has ruled. This is the full case file, from the public record.

Chapters
0:00 7,624 tickets
0:15 The limit
0:41 The scale
1:19 The names
1:51 The Error Bible
2:17 The tabs
2:43 Verify you are a human
3:25 What they knew
3:56 Bottom line

What the record is. The case is a complaint, filed 15 October 2026 in the Southern District of California: everything in it is an allegation by the United States, not a finding, and the FTC's release says the case will be decided by the court. The complaint names REPS and three of its officers. Ticketmaster, AXS and the resale sites are not defendants; their ticket limits are the ones the complaint says were evaded. Our earlier Ticketmaster file was a different case. The FTC release places the stadium concert in Kansas City; we do not name the performer. The complaint prints at least 83,000 events in one paragraph and at least 83,500 in another (the FTC release uses 83,500); we say at least 83,000. About $6.53 of profit a ticket overall, about $109 a ticket at the stadium concert, and at least 953 buyers' worth at the top limit are our arithmetic from the complaint's numbers. The complaint does not use the word bot; it does allege that some account creation and the collection of verification codes were automated. The 40% slowdown is REPS's own assessment, as the complaint describes it. The Maryland ruling (April 2026) came in a separate FTC case against another broker: it denied that broker's motion to dismiss, it is quoted as Pollstar and Music Business Worldwide report it, and it does not decide this case. REPS's statements are as reported by TicketNews. The government asks for a permanent injunction, monetary relief and civil penalties for each violation; no amount is named and nothing has been awarded. Status as of 14 November 2026: the FTC case page reads Pending, and we found no answer, motion, ruling or settlement.

FTC case page, REPS & Company, Inc., U.S. v., matter 252 3105: https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/cases-proceedings/252-3105-reps-company-inc-us-v

metadata.title: The $1.3 Billion Ticket Rig: How Ticketmaster & Scalper Bots Harvest Live Events
metadata.author: Veridox
metadata.shortDescription:
The $1.3 Billion Ticket Rig: How Ticketmaster & Scalper Bots Harvest Live Events

Why do face-value concert tickets vanish seconds after they go on sale, only to reappear on resale at two, three, or ten times the price?

In this Veridox investigative documentary, we follow the paper trail across four federal dockets to show how an eighty percent ticketing primary market and a billion-dollar broker shadow market turned live events into a harvesting machine.

What the evidence establishes:
- Ticketmaster and Live Nation control more than eighty percent of major U.S. concert venue primary ticketing.
- Between 2019 and 2024, the company collected sixteen point four billion dollars in mandatory drip fees, often twenty-four to forty-four percent of the ticket face value.
- Internal documents show staff called drip pricing bait and switch and described the checkout experience as sucks.
- A 2018 internal exhibit tracked broker R-E-P-S controlling one thousand seventy-four accounts holding one hundred two thousand nine hundred sixty-eight tickets across one thousand two hundred two events, worth roughly fourteen point eight million dollars.
- From January 2022 through October 2025, R-E-P-S spent more than one point three billion dollars acquiring more than eighteen point five million tickets across more than eighty-three thousand five hundred events, clearing at least one hundred twenty point eight million dollars in resale profit.
- For one Beyoncé show at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City on October 1, 2023, more than thirteen hundred accounts bought seven thousand six hundred twenty-four tickets, roughly eight hundred thirty-three thousand three hundred twenty-three dollars in profit.
- For one Pitbull show at Empower FCU Amphitheater on September 7, 2024, more than seven hundred accounts bought five thousand four hundred thirty tickets, roughly thirty-one percent of the venue, roughly one hundred twenty thousand one hundred nine dollars in profit.
- Broker mechanics included power of attorney forms, Automatiq-style bot tools, virtual credit cards, SIM banks, rotating IP proxies, multi-session browsers, and an internal Error Bible.
- R-E-P-S President Brian Archibald said on October 16, 2026: We use real people, using real accounts, to purchase tickets. We never use bots.
- The F-T-C and seven states sued Live Nation and Ticketmaster in September 2025. On September 28, 2026, the court ruled the BOTS Act does not preclude platforms from facing liability.
- The Department of Justice and thirty-nine states plus D.C. sued Live Nation and Ticketmaster. A Manhattan jury found Live Nation liable on all counts on April 15, 2026, awarding one dollar and seventy-two cents per ticket across twenty-one states plus D.C., up to roughly four hundred fifty million dollars trebled.
- Thirty-three states settled mid-trial for two hundred eighty point four million dollars, thirteen amphitheaters to be divested, a fifteen percent amphitheater fee cap, an open API, and an eight-year decree.
- Thirty-three non-settling state attorneys general plus D.C. won the verdict and are pursuing a February 2027 structural breakup trial.
- Live Nation says it invested more than one billion dollars in anti-bot technology, blocks more than ninety-nine percent of twenty-five million daily signup attempts, blocked eight point seven billion bot access attempts in April 2025, retired TradeDesk, restricted brokers to one taxpayer-ID verified account, and adopted all-in pricing in May 2025.
- Whether these lawsuits break the ticket rig for fans is not proved until three courtroom tests play out: the Tunney Act review of the DOJ settlement, full discovery before Judge Frimpong in Los Angeles, and the R-E-P-S and Key Investment Group cases in San Diego and Maryland.

This film is built on court complaints, jury verdicts, court orders, and internal company documents. Where the record is contested, we present each side in neutral terms. Nothing here is legal advice.

Chapters:
0:00 The ten A.M. ticket queue
1:48 The eighty percent ticketing monopoly
3:36 The hidden drip fee machine
5:24 The broker shadow market
7:12 The Error Bible
9:00 The federal lawsuits
10:48 The defense case
12:36 The verdict and the twenty twenty-seven tests
14:24 Who actually pays

#Veridox #Ticketmaster #LiveNation #ScalperBots #ConcertTickets #BOTSAct #Antitrust #FTC #DOJ #TicketResale #DripFees #TicketRig #FeeTrap #LiveEvents #InvestigativeDocumentary #TicketmasterLawsuit #ConcertMonopoly #Scalping #PrimaryTicketing #SecondaryMarket #AllInPricing #TradeDesk #BrokerAccounts #FanVerification

metadata.author: Intuit
metadata.shortDescription:
Not sure whether a business credit card or a business line of credit is right for your small business?

This video breaks down the key differences—from how each one works to when to use them. You'll learn about interest costs, convenience, and which option may fit your everyday spending or larger funding needs, with help from Intuit tools to track every dollar.

00:41 - How business credit cards work for everyday spending2

01:08 - How interest accrues on credit lines vs. credit cards4
02:09 - Comparing convenience: instant swipes vs. bank transfers5
02:38 - Best use cases for cards and lines of credit6
02:59 - Using financial tools to track business expenses

In this video, a small retail shop owner shares her firsthand experience choosing between a business credit card and a line of credit to fund renovations, inventory, and seasonal staffing. It covers:

• How credit cards work for everyday purchases and rewards.
• How lines of credit provide a flexible pool of funds for bigger expenses/
• The difference in interest: credit card rates vs. interest that starts accruing the moment you draw from a line of credit.
• Why a credit card offers instant access while a line of credit requires a transfer step.
• When to use each: daily operating costs vs. bulk inventory, seasonal gaps, or unexpected repairs.

Plus, find out how Intuit QuickBooks helps organize your financial data so your credit purchases and other expenses are easy to access and categorize.

View the video to learn more about filling out your business tax return.

And don’t forget to like, comment, and subscribe for more small business tax tips and how-to videos.

metadata.title: Where Your Ticket Fees Actually Go
metadata.author: Checkout Math
metadata.shortDescription:
Government auditors found ticket fees averaging 27% of the price on original sales and 31% on resale sites. We look at who sets and keeps those fees, what Ticketmaster earned in 2025, why fees climb along with ticket prices, what the FTC's all-in price rule changed, and where the Live Nation antitrust case stands after the 2026 jury verdict.

In this video:
• how big ticket fees are;
• who keeps the fee: venues or Ticketmaster;
• Ticketmaster's 2025 numbers, per ticket;
• why fees grow with ticket prices;
• the FTC rule that took effect in May 2025;
• resale prices and the FTC lawsuit;
• the DOJ settlement and the jury verdict.

What's the biggest ticket fee you ever paid, and what was the show? Tell me in the comments.

Not financial or legal advice. Narration: synthetic voice.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
0:41 How big the fees are
1:39 Who keeps the fee
2:19 What Ticketmaster makes
3:09 Why the fee keeps growing
4:10 The all-in price rule
5:36 The monopoly case
7:03 The checkout math

#ticketfees #ticketmaster #checkoutmath

segments.text: In 2018, government auditors looked at the fees on tickets for concerts and games.
On the original sale, fees added an average of 27% to the ticket price.
On resale sites, the average was 31%.
At that rate, a $100 ticket really costs about $127 at checkout.
So who gets the extra money?
To find out, we read the Government Accountability Office report,
Live Nation's financial results, testimony to the Senate,
the Federal Trade Commission's fee rule and its lawsuit,
and the antitrust case that went to trial this year.
Start with the size.
The Government Accountability Office is the investigative arm of Congress,
and it published its ticketing report in April 2018.
In the events it reviewed, total fees averaged 27% of the ticket price on the original
sale and 31% on resale sites.
Some resale sites charged more than 40%.
Some websites showed the fees only after the buyer had typed in payment information.
The auditors said their sample wasn't designed to represent every event,
so treat those numbers as a snapshot.
In September 2025, the Federal Trade Commission and seven states sued Live Nation
and Ticketmaster.
The FTC alleged that Ticketmaster's mandatory fees could reach 44% of a ticket's
cost, and that those fees added up to $16.4 billion from 2019
through 2024.
None of that has been proven in court, and the case is still open.
So who keeps the fee?
Ticketmaster gave its answer to the Senate in January 2023,
after the Taylor Swift presale meltdown.
Live Nation president Joe Berchtold testified that in most cases the venues set
the fees and keep most of the money, and that the share Ticketmaster keeps has been
falling.
Senators pushed back.
Committee chair Dick Durbin asked him, you control the venue,
do you not?
Berchtold answered that Live Nation owns only about 5% of U.S.
venues.
Whoever keeps the larger cut, the buyer sees one fee line at checkout,
with the venue's share and the ticket company's share inside it.
Ticketmaster's own share is still a big business.
In 2025, Live Nation's ticketing segment, which is Ticketmaster,
brought in about $3.1 billion in revenue and about 1.1 billion in
adjusted operating income.
That's a margin of 37%.
It handled 346 million tickets that carried a fee.
Divide it out, and Ticketmaster brought in roughly $8.90 in revenue for each of
those tickets, with about $3.30 left as adjusted operating income.
That's our own math, and the revenue includes more than fees,
so take it as a rough scale.
The whole company had about $25.2 billion in revenue last year,
and ticketing alone produced almost half of its total adjusted operating income.
Fees often grow every year because they are usually set as a percentage of the ticket
price.
When the price goes up, the fee goes up with it, and prices for big shows climbed
fast.
Pollstar, the concert industry's trade publication,
tracks the one hundred biggest tours in the world.
In 2019, their average ticket cost $96.17.
Those numbers are worldwide and cover only the top tours,
so smaller shows can look very different.
Over the same five years, overall U.S.
consumer prices rose about 23%.
If that average ticket had only kept up with inflation,
it would have cost about $118.
Now add a 27% fee.
On the 2019 price, that's about $26.
On the 2024 price, it's about $37.
In 2025 the average dipped slightly, as the top tours sold fewer tickets.
For years, the fee often showed up only at the end.
The site listed one price, and the real total appeared at checkout.
Regulators call that drip pricing.
On May twelfth, 2025, an FTC rule took effect for live event tickets and short-term
rentals.
Sellers now have to show the total price up front, including mandatory fees,
and make it more prominent than other prices.
They also have to say what each fee is for.
The rule sets no limit on the size of a fee.
A seller can still charge 30%, as long as it's inside the first price you see.
Government taxes, shipping and optional extras can still be left out of that number.
So the rule makes fees easier to compare, and the fees themselves can stay just
as big.
Resale adds another layer.
In one sold-out rock concert the GAO looked at, original tickets cost between $50
and one hundred dollars, and resale prices ran from $90 up to $790.
The FTC's lawsuit also alleges that Ticketmaster let brokers get around its ticket
limits.
It cites an internal review that found five brokers controlling 6,345 accounts,
and it says Ticketmaster earns fees on resales as well.
The complaint quotes an internal email in which an executive wrote that the companies
turn a blind eye, as a matter of policy, to brokers breaking the posted limits.
The biggest fight is over competition.
In May 2024, the Justice Department and dozens of states sued Live Nation,
arguing that it illegally dominates live events through Ticketmaster,
its concert promotion and its venues.
The trial began on March second, 2026.
Six days later, the Justice Department announced a settlement.
Under the proposed deal, Live Nation would sell thirteen amphitheaters,
cap Ticketmaster's fees at 15% at the amphitheaters it owns,
and set up a settlement fund of about $280 million.
It would keep Ticketmaster.
The deal still needs a judge's approval, and the judge called the way it was announced
completely unacceptable.
Most of the states refused the deal and kept going.
On April fifteenth, 2026, a federal jury in Manhattan found that Ticketmaster
illegally maintained a monopoly in ticketing for major concert venues,
and that fans paid more because of it.
The jury also found that Live Nation has a monopoly over large amphitheaters and
unlawfully requires artists who play them to use its promotion services.
New York's attorney general said fans in that state were overcharged $1.72
per ticket in higher fees.
Live Nation said it would appeal.
In the latest reports we found, the judge had not yet ruled on penalties or on a
breakup.
So where does your ticket fee go?
First, it's large, around a quarter to a third of the ticket price in the government's
sample.
Second, it's split, with venues often keeping most of it,
while Ticketmaster still earns more than a billion dollars a year in adjusted operating
income.
Third, fees climb along with ticket prices, and the federal rule only makes them
visible.
What can you do with that?
Compare the total price, which sellers now have to show first,
across the official seller and the resale sites.
Read what each fee is for, since the rule makes sellers explain it.
And on resale listings, look at the final amount before you commit.
Next on Checkout Math: the money behind self-storage units.
If you want that one, subscribe.
And tell me in the comments: what's the biggest ticket fee you ever paid,
and what was the show?

Committee chair Dick Durbin asked him, you control the venue, do you not? Berchtold answered that Live Nation owns only about 5% of U.S. venues. Whoever keeps the larger cut, the buyer sees one fee line at checkout, with the venue's share and the ticket company's share inside it. Ticketmaster's own share is still a big business. In 2025, Live Nation's ticketing segment, which is Ticketmaster, brought in about $3.1 billion in revenue and about 1.1 billion in adjusted operating income. That's a margin of 37%. It handled 346 million tickets that carried a fee. Divide it out, and Ticketmaster brought in roughly $8.90 in revenue for each of those tickets, with about $3.30 left as adjusted operating income. That's our own math, and the revenue includes more than fees, so take it as a rough scale. The whole company had about $25.2 billion in revenue last year, and ticketing alone produced almost half of its total adjusted operating income. Fees often grow every year because they are usually set as a percentage of the ticket price. When the price goes up, the fee goes up with it, and prices for big shows climbed fast. Pollstar, the concert industry's trade publication, tracks the one hundred biggest tours in the world. In 2019, their average ticket cost $96.17. By 2024, it cost $135.92, up 41%. Those numbers are worldwide and cover only the top tours, so smaller shows can look very different. Over the same five years, overall U.S. consumer prices rose about 23%. If that average ticket had only kept up with inflation, it would have cost about $118. Now add a 27% fee. On the 2019 price, that's about $26. On the 2024 price, it's about $37. In 2025 the average dipped slightly, as the top tours sold fewer tickets. For years, the fee often showed up only at the end. The site listed one price, and the real total appeared at checkout. Regulators call that drip pricing. On May twelfth, 2025, an FTC rule took effect for live event tickets and short-term rentals. Sellers now have to show the total price up front, including mandatory fees, and make it more prominent than other prices. They also have to say what each fee is for. The rule sets no limit on the size of a fee. A seller can still charge 30%, as long as it's inside the first price you see. Government taxes, shipping and optional extras can still be left out of that number. So the rule makes fees easier to compare, and the fees themselves can stay just as big. Resale adds another layer. In one sold-out rock concert the GAO looked at, original tickets cost between $50 and one hundred dollars, and resale prices ran from $90 up to $790. The FTC's lawsuit also alleges that Ticketmaster let brokers get around its ticket limits. It cites an internal review that found five brokers controlling 6,345 accounts, and it says Ticketmaster earns fees on resales as well. The complaint quotes an internal email in which an executive wrote that the companies turn a blind eye, as a matter of policy, to brokers breaking the posted limits. The biggest fight is over competition. In May 2024, the Justice Department and dozens of states sued Live Nation, arguing that it illegally dominates live events through Ticketmaster, its concert promotion and its venues. The trial began on March second, 2026. Six days later, the Justice Department announced a settlement. Under the proposed deal, Live Nation would sell thirteen amphitheaters, cap Ticketmaster's fees at 15% at the amphitheaters it owns, and set up a settlement fund of about $280 million. It would keep Ticketmaster. The deal still needs a judge's approval, and the judge called the way it was announced completely unacceptable. Most of the states refused the deal and kept going. On April fifteenth, 2026, a federal jury in Manhattan found that Ticketmaster illegally maintained a monopoly in ticketing for major concert venues, and that fans paid more because of it. The jury also found that Live Nation has a monopoly over large amphitheaters and unlawfully requires artists who play them to use its promotion services. New York's attorney general said fans in that state were overcharged $1.72 per ticket in higher fees. Live Nation said it would appeal. In the latest reports we found, the judge had not yet ruled on penalties or on a breakup. So where does your ticket fee go? First, it's large, around a quarter to a third of the ticket price in the government's sample. Second, it's split, with venues often keeping most of it, while Ticketmaster still earns more than a billion dollars a year in adjusted operating income. Third, fees climb along with ticket prices, and the federal rule only makes them visible. What can you do with that? Compare the total price, which sellers now have to show first, across the official seller and the resale sites. Read what each fee is for, since the rule makes sellers explain it. And on resale listings, look at the final amount before you commit. Next on Checkout Math: the money behind self-storage units. If you want that one, subscribe. And tell me in the comments: what's the biggest ticket fee you ever paid, and what was the show?

metadata.title: How To Buy Presale Tickets On Ticketmaster (2026) (Complete Guide)
metadata.author: Three Step Guide
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn how to buy presale tickets on Ticketmaster with this complete guide. This tutorial shows you how to buy presale tickets on Ticketmaster, use presale access, and complete your purchase on Ticketmaster using the latest 2026 method. Perfect for beginners who want early ticket access.

Hashtags:
#Ticketmaster #Presale #Tickets #Events #Guide #Tutorial #BuyTickets
keywords: how to buy presale tickets on ticketmaster

segments.text: Hello, today we will guide you through
how to buy pre-sale tickets on
Ticketmaster. To get started, open the
Ticketmaster PH website in your browser.
Once the homepage loads, take a moment
to get familiar with the layout. This is
where you can browse available events,
including concerts, sports, and
festivals.
If you are purchasing during a pre-sale
window, it is a good idea to have your
account ready and stay alert since
popular events can move quickly.
From the homepage, click on the sample
event shown on screen.
This will open the events detail page
where you can review important
information such as the event date,
venue, and any available ticket options.
Before moving forward, make sure you are
on the correct event page, especially if
there are multiple dates or similar
listings.
Next, scroll down until you see the find
tickets button, then click it. This
takes you into the ticket selection
area.
Depending on demand, the page may take a
few moments to load, so be patient and
avoid refreshing unless absolutely
necessary. Refreshing during
high-traffic sales can sometimes
interrupt your progress. Once you are in
the ticketing section, select the sample
ticket. At this stage, you may see
different seating sections, pricing
tiers, or availability options.
Choose the option that matches what you
want. If you are aiming to complete your
purchase quickly, it helps to already
know your preferred budget or seating
area before you start.
After that, click on best available.
This option is useful if you want the
system to automatically assign the best
tickets currently available based on the
events inventory. It can save time
during pre-sale purchases, especially
when tickets are selling fast. If the
exact seats you want are unavailable,
this is often one of the quickest ways
to continue. From there, follow the
on-screen procedure to complete the
process. The system will guide you
through the remaining steps, which may
include confirming your ticket
selection, reviewing your order, and
proceeding through checkout.
Read each screen carefully before
continuing and double-check the details
shown, including ticket quantity,
section, and total cost.
As a final tip, move through each page
promptly but carefully. Presale tickets
are often limited, so timing matters,
but accuracy is just as important. Make
sure your internet connection is stable
and your payment method is ready before
you begin. With that, you should be all
set to buy presale tickets on
Ticketmaster quickly and smoothly.

metadata.title: How One Company Bought 18.5 Million Tickets Before You Could
metadata.author: The Empire Files
metadata.shortDescription:
On October 15, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice sued REPS & Company and three of its executives, alleging they used thousands of accounts, virtual credit cards, and technology to defeat ticket-purchase limits — and bought more than 18.5 million tickets.

Everything in this video comes from the government's complaint. Nothing here is a court finding. No liability has been found, and there is no refund program for fans.

Chapters:
0:00 Cold Open — The Night the Seats Vanished
0:53 The Machine
2:33 The Scale
4:42 The Law
6:43 So What

Sources:
- U.S. Department of Justice complaint against REPS & Company, Inc., filed October 15, 2026, U.S. District Court, Southern District of California, Case No. 3:26-cv-05895-CAB-BJW
- Federal Trade Commission announcement, October 15, 2026 (FTC voted 2-0 to refer the matter to the DOJ)
- The BOTS Act (Better Online Ticket Sales Act, 2016)

The figures in this video — more than $1.3 billion spent, more than 18.5 million tickets, at least 83,500 events, at least $120.8 million in alleged resale profit — are allegations in the complaint, not proven facts. The Beyoncé example (October 1, 2023, Kansas City: 1,300+ accounts, 7,624 tickets, about $833,323 alleged resale profit) is also drawn from the complaint.

This video is an independent explainer. It is not affiliated with the Department of Justice, the FTC, REPS & Company, Ticketmaster, or any artist named.

#TheEmpireFiles

segments.text: One night, one concert, 7,624
tickets,
all bought before real fans got a
chance.
October 1st, 2023,
Beyoncé takes the stage in Kansas City.
Fans refreshed the page again and again.
The site said sold out,
but the seats were not gone to luckier
fans. They were gone to one company.
The government says that company used
more than 1,300 fake accounts to buy
them all,
then resold them for a profit of
This is the story of REPS and how the
ticket game is really played.
The seats were gone while real fans were
still in line, and this was not one
concert.
It was 83,500
events.
To understand what happened, you have to
understand the limit.
When tickets go on sale, Ticketmaster
and AXS cap how many one buyer can take,
usually eight.
The limit exists for one reason, so one
buyer cannot take everything.
The complaint says REPS treated that
limit as a puzzle to solve.
Thousands of online accounts, virtual
credit cards, employees overseas working
around the clock.
Each account bought a few tickets.
Together, they bought millions.
The idea is simple, defeat the controls
that enforce the limit.
This is not a new trick.
In 2016, Congress passed a law against
it, the BOTS Act.
It came after bots swept up tickets for
hit shows, and fans were left with
nothing.
The law bans circumventing the systems
that enforce posted purchase limits.
Ticket sellers built their own defenses,
too, queues, verified fan lists,
captchas.
The government says REPS built a to get
past all of them.
And the tickets did not stay with reps.
They flowed to resale sites.
StubHub, Vivid Seats, SeatGeek,
GameTime, TicketNetwork, even
Ticketmaster's own resale platform.
Those platforms are not accused of
anything. The complaint names only reps
and its three executives.
Think of it like this. The limit is a
door that lets eight people through at a
time.
Reps, the government says, walked
through it 1,300 times at once.
Now the scale, because the numbers are
hard to believe.
Between January 2022 and October 2025,
the complaint says reps spent more than
$1.3 billion buying tickets.
More than 18.5 million tickets for at
least 83,500
events.
Concerts, sports, shows of every kind.
The resale profit, the government says,
was at least $120.8
million.
That is profit alleged in a complaint,
not a court finding,
not a fine, an allegation.
Take the Beyoncé show apart. 7,624
tickets, about $109 of alleged profit on
each one.
At another show, the complaint says 700
accounts bought 5,430
tickets, about $120,000 in profit.
One show, then another, then 83,000
more.
The three men named are the chief
executive, Ryan PenCheff, the president,
Brian Archibald, and the chief operating
officer, Nicholas Totarande.
The company is Reps and Company, based
in San Diego.
The complaint is 22 pages long, one
count, violating the Bots Act and the
FTC Act.
And the Beyoncé show was not the only
one. The complaint names Post Malone,
Luke Bryan, Pitbull, and thousands more.
For fans, the math is simple.
Every ticket a broker takes is a ticket
a fan cannot buy at the real price.
The government says the buying ran for
almost four years. 3.1 million separate
purchases.
That is not a fan who got lucky. That is
a system running every day.
And every one of those purchases started
the same way. A fan in a queue watching
the seats disappear.
The money did not vanish. It moved from
fans to a broker, to a resale site.
Follow it and you find the machine.
So what happens now?
The case was filed on October 15th,
The Justice Department filed it after
the FTC voted two to zero to refer it.
It is in federal court in San Diego.
Case number three 26 CV 05895.
The government wants three things.
A permanent injunction,
monetary relief, and civil penalties.
An injunction means a court order to
stop.
Monetary relief means paying money back.
Civil penalties mean fines.
But here is what the case is not. It is
not a verdict.
No court has ruled. No liability has
been found. And there is no refund
program for fans.
What happens next is slow and mostly
paperwork. Reps answers the complaint.
Both sides exchange evidence. A judge
decides what is proven.
That can take months.
Sometimes years.
The FTC has been moving this way for a
while. It has used the Bots Act before.
And this case is separate from the
bigger Ticketmaster lawsuit filed in
September 2025.
Different defendants,
different claims.
That matters because it is easy to blur
every ticket story into one. They are
not one story.
What the government must now prove is
the method.
That the accounts, the cards, the
technology were used to defeat the
limits.
Reps has not yet filed its response.
When it does, that is where its side
will be heard.
As of the last public check in October,
no response had been filed.
Reps has not been found guilty of
anything. That sentence belongs in every
honest version of this story.
The complaint is the beginning. The
courtroom is where it gets tested.
And the docket is public. Anyone can
watch it move.
So what does all of this mean for you?
First, the ticket you want is not only
competing with other fans, it is
competing with machines.
That is not your fault, and it is not a
reason to give up on live music.
Second, the law is catching up slowly.
The BOTS Act exists. The FTC is using
it, and this case will test how far it
reaches.
Third, the price you see is not always
the price.
Resale markups, fees, and dynamic
pricing all sit between you and the
seat.
What can you actually do? A few things.
Buy only from the official seller when
you can.
Set a price limit before the sale
starts, and walk away when it passes.
If a site lets you join the wait list
instead of the resale market.
And if a ticket looks too cheap to be
true,
it probably is.
None of this fixes the system, but it
keeps you from paying the most for it.
The bigger fix is not yours to make. It
belongs to the platforms, the sellers,
and the courts.
Platforms can enforce their own limits.
Sellers can sell fairly. Courts can
decide what the law means.
Until then, the story is not over. The
complaint is filed. The docket is open.
The next chapter is a courtroom.
We will follow it, because the money
always leaves a trail.
If this helped you see the ticket game
differently, subscribe.
The next case is already on the docket.
And if you have ever lost a ticket to a
bot, tell us in the comments.
We read everyone.
This is the Empire Files. We follow the
money.

metadata.title: The Next Vivid Seats Costs $4.83 — The Ticketing Stock Growing 7% With No Rescue Deal
metadata.author: KC_Watermark
metadata.shortDescription:
Vivid Seats (NASDAQ: SEAT) popped about 60% premarket on Thursday, November 19, 2026, after announcing a Transaction Support Agreement with its lenders — a rescue that cuts net debt by about $232M (from ~$342M to ~$110M) but converts about $273M of debt into about 45.8M new shares, leaving lenders with about 80% of the equity and existing holders with about 20%. This video asks the follow-up question: is there a ticketing stock with a bid under it that does NOT need a dilutive rescue?

StubHub Holdings (NYSE: STUB), the headline peer: the global secondary-ticketing marketplace (StubHub + viagogo) — the closest business model to Vivid on the board. Closed Wednesday, November 18 at $4.83 (+6.62%); trading about $4.81 Thursday morning; market cap about $1.73B — larger than Vivid, the sector anchor. Q3 2026 (reported November 10): revenue $501.95M, up +7.2% year over year; EPS $0.10; about $1.2B of cash at September 30. The stock is down about -64% year to date and printed its 52-week low of $4.51 on November 17 (52-week high $16.63). The flag, on screen in the video: StubHub carries heavy losses of its own on a trailing-twelve-month basis (EPS TTM about -$1.45) — "cleaner than SEAT today" is a relative claim, and it is stated as one.

Eventbrite (NYSE: EB), the affordable contrast peer: about $4.51 a share, market cap about $440M. Self-service PRIMARY ticketing for event creators — the other side of the market from the SEAT/STUB resale model. Annual revenue about $294.8M (roughly 1.5x sales); net loss about -$15.6M TTM; and no $342M net-debt recap hanging over it. The flag, hard, on screen: Eventbrite's revenue has SHRUNK, from about $326M to about $292M, and it is still loss-making — a smaller, quieter business, not a growth story.

Vivid, ticker SEAT, announced a rescue deal with its lenders at six thirty this morning.
The deal cuts its net debt by about two hundred thirty-two million dollars, from about three hundred forty-two million down to about one hundred ten million.
That sounds like good news, and the stock treated it that way.
But read the other half of the deal.
About two hundred seventy-three million dollars of debt turns into about forty-five point eight million brand-new shares.
When it closes, the lenders own about eighty percent of the company, and the people who own the stock today keep about twenty percent.
So here is the question this video walks through, in order.
Is there a ticketing stock with a bid under it that does not need a rescue like that?
Two names, both under five dollars — and every flag goes on the screen.
Name one is the closest thing to Vivid Seats in the whole market.
StubHub, ticker STUB — the resale marketplace, StubHub here and viagogo overseas, where fans buy and sell tickets to live events in more than two hundred countries.
It is the same basic business as Vivid: a secondary-ticketing marketplace that takes its cut when a ticket changes hands.
StubHub closed Wednesday at four dollars and eighty-three cents, up six point six two percent on the day, and it was trading around four dollars and eighty-one cents this morning.

At about one point seven three billion dollars of market value, StubHub is actually bigger than Vivid Seats.
This is the anchor name in the sector, not a tiny upstart.
It just happens to trade at four eighty-three, near the bottom of its range.
Now the quarter, because this is where StubHub separates itself from Vivid.
StubHub reported third quarter results on November tenth.
Revenue came in at five hundred one point nine five million dollars, up seven point two percent from a year ago.
Earnings were ten cents a share.
And the company was holding about one point two billion dollars in cash at the end of September.
Put that next to Vivid's third quarter, reported November ninth.
Vivid's revenue was one hundred twenty-six point nine million, down seven percent, with a net loss of seventeen point four million.
Same industry, same quarter, opposite directions.
One of these two resale marketplaces is still growing its top line, and it is not the one that needed a lender rescue this morning.
That growth — seven point two percent, already printed — is the headline of this video, and it is why StubHub leads it.
So why is a growing name this cheap?
Look at the chart, because the chart is rough.
StubHub is down about sixty-four percent year to date.
On November seventeenth, two days ago, it printed its fifty-two week low at four dollars and fifty-one cents, against a fifty-two week high of sixteen dollars and sixty-three cents.
This stock has been left for dead.
Wednesday it bounced six point six two percent, and there were reports of insiders buying shares this week — at least somebody with a name putting money down near the lows.
But here is the line that matters for this video.
There is no rescue deal hanging over StubHub.
No transaction support agreement.
No pile of new shares promised to lenders.
No eighty-twenty split waiting to close in the first quarter.
Whatever StubHub's problems are — and it has one big one, coming up next — a dilutive lender recap is not one of them today.
Now the flag on StubHub, and we put it on the screen in red like every flag here.
StubHub loses money.
Over the last twelve months its losses have been heavy — earnings per share on a trailing basis sit around minus one dollar and forty-five cents in the market data we pulled this morning.
This is not a profitable company trading cheap.
It is a growing company that is still carrying heavy losses, and the stock being down sixty-four percent this year is the market pricing exactly that.
So when we say StubHub looks cleaner than Vivid Seats today, hear that the right way.
Cleaner is a relative claim.
Vivid needed its lenders to take eighty percent of the company to keep the balance sheet standing.
StubHub has not needed that.
That is the whole claim — relative, not clean.
Anybody who tells you this name is flag-free is selling something.
Name two is the affordable peer, and it plays a different position.
Eventbrite, ticker EB, trades at four dollars and fifty-one cents a share, with a market value of about four hundred forty million dollars — about a quarter of StubHub's size.
Eventbrite is not a resale marketplace.
It is primary ticketing: the self-service platform event creators use to sell tickets to their own events in the first place — the local concert, the food festival, the class, the small venue show.
StubHub and Vivid fight over tickets that already exist.
Eventbrite helps create the tickets.
Annual revenue runs about two hundred ninety-four point eight million dollars, so the stock trades at roughly one and a half times sales.
And the point for this video: there is no three hundred forty-two million dollar net-debt rescue hanging over Eventbrite.
No lender deal.
No eighty-twenty split.
If this morning's pop says ticketing stocks have a bid under them again, Eventbrite is the small one that does not need a rescue to be part of that conversation.
And now Eventbrite's flags, plural, because this one has them and they go on the screen hard.
Flag one: this business is shrinking.
Eventbrite's annual revenue has come down from about three hundred twenty-six million dollars to about two hundred ninety-two million.
That is the wrong direction, and it is the main reason the stock is four dollars and fifty-one cents.
Flag two: it is still losing money — a net loss of about fifteen point six million dollars over the last twelve months.
Smaller losses than the other two names here, but losses all the same.
So be clear about what Eventbrite is.
It is a smaller, quieter business on the other side of the ticketing market, with no rescue deal over it — and a revenue line that has to stop shrinking before it is anything more than that.
It is not a growth story, and we are not going to dress it up as one.
Put the three side by side and the morning makes sense.
Vivid Seats popped about sixty percent — on a rescue that hands its lenders about eighty percent of the company and leaves today's holders with about twenty.
The pop is real, and so is the dilution; both numbers belong on the screen at the same time.
StubHub, the same resale model, closed at four eighty-three with revenue growing seven point two percent and no rescue announced — but with heavy losses of its own, down sixty-four percent this year.
Eventbrite sits at four fifty-one with no debt recap over it — but with revenue shrinking from three twenty-six to two ninety-two, and a fifteen point six million dollar loss.
That is the honest board.
Ticketing has a bid under it again this morning.
Not one of these three names is flag-free, and the flags are the difference between a story and a sales pitch.
So here is how we grade it from here.
On StubHub: watch whether that seven point two percent revenue growth holds in the next quarter, and whether the losses narrow.
Growth with narrowing losses is a real story; growth with widening losses is just a bigger version of the same problem.
And watch whether it holds above that four fifty-one low from November seventeenth.
On Eventbrite: one number matters most — revenue has to stop shrinking.
Two ninety-two has to flatten, then turn, or the quiet-business case stays just that: quiet.

And on Vivid: the rescue is expected to close in the first quarter of twenty twenty-seven, and the stock now trades on whether twenty percent of a deleveraged company is worth more than all of a drowning one.
Our verdict: Vivid Seats needed a rescue.
StubHub is growing seven percent without one, at four eighty-three — and Eventbrite is the four fifty-one name with no rescue and a shrinking business to fix.
Flags and all, that is the board.
Like, subscribe, and share it with someone who buys their tickets on one of these apps — and we will see you at the next report.

It is not a growth story, and we are not going to dress it up as one. Put the three side by side and the morning makes sense. Vivid Seats popped about sixty percent — on a rescue that hands its lenders about eighty percent of the company and leaves today's holders with about twenty. The pop is real, and so is the dilution; both numbers belong on the screen at the same time. StubHub, the same resale model, closed at four eighty-three with revenue growing seven point two percent and no rescue announced — but with heavy losses of its own, down sixty-four percent this year. Eventbrite sits at four fifty-one with no debt recap over it — but with revenue shrinking from three twenty-six to two ninety-two, and a fifteen point six million dollar loss. That is the honest board. Ticketing has a bid under it again this morning. Not one of these three names is flag-free, and the flags are the difference between a story and a sales pitch. So here is how we grade it from here. On StubHub: watch whether that seven point two percent revenue growth holds in the next quarter, and whether the losses narrow. Growth with narrowing losses is a real story; growth with widening losses is just a bigger version of the same problem. And watch whether it holds above that four fifty-one low from November seventeenth. On Eventbrite: one number matters most — revenue has to stop shrinking. Two ninety-two has to flatten, then turn, or the quiet-business case stays just that: quiet. And on Vivid: the rescue is expected to close in the first quarter of twenty twenty-seven, and the stock now trades on whether twenty percent of a deleveraged company is worth more than all of a drowning one. Our verdict: Vivid Seats needed a rescue. StubHub is growing seven percent without one, at four eighty-three — and Eventbrite is the four fifty-one name with no rescue and a shrinking business to fix. Flags and all, that is the board. Like, subscribe, and share it with someone who buys their tickets on one of these apps — and we will see you at the next report.

Learn how to accept your electronic ticket transfer from SeatGeek through Vivid Seats. 

You’ll receive an order confirmation email and a second email that explains how to accept your SeatGeek tickets once they’ve been transferred. First, log in to your SeatGeek account. If your SeatGeek and Vivid Seats emails match, your tickets will automatically appear. It can take some time for your tickets to be transferred, but with our 100% Buyer Guarantee you’re protected and you’ll get into your event.

If you don’t have an account, create one. Be sure to use the same email you used to purchase tickets on Vivid Seats. When your tickets are ready, you’ll get a heads up from Vivid Seats and SeatGeek. 

To access your tickets, log in to your new account. You’ll see the name of your event and an event image. Click the image to access your tickets. To make the ticket code bigger and more scannable or send tickets to a friend, tap the QR code.

You’ll need to show the tickets on a mobile device to get into your event. Make sure you’re logged into seatgeek.com and can access your tickets on your phone before the event.

TROUBLESHOOTING TIPS
0:00 - Intro
2:19 - Emails don’t match 
2:37 - Tickets not loading in app

If you’re having trouble accessing your SeatGeek tickets, double check that your email addresses match up on Vivid Seats and SeatGeek. Try refreshing your browser or using a different one. Make sure to access your tickets from your phone and not a desktop.
If you can’t find your tickets, double check that you received an email from Vivid Seats confirming the ticket transfer. Reminder, your tickets won’t necessarily transfer the day you purchased them but they’re on their way.

metadata.title: What Is Speculative Ticketing? Unauthorized Ticket Resale Explained
metadata.author: TicketSpice
metadata.shortDescription:
Speculative ticketing, also known as ghost ticketing, is when unauthorized third-party sellers list or sell tickets they do not actually have, often at a much higher price than the official ticket page.

In this video, TicketSpice Co-founder Eric Knopf explains how speculative ticketing works, why it creates problems for event organizers, attraction operators, fans, and attendees, and how it can lead to higher ticket prices, confusion at checkout, and a worse guest experience.

If this is happening to your event or attraction, reach out to our team. We can help you protect your ticket sales and your attendees.

Learn more at ticketspice.com
