metadata.title: Credit Cards For Beginners cash back vs travels. No annual fee
metadata.author: The Money Advantage
metadata.shortDescription:
Master your finances with this 8-minute guide to choosing your first credit card! We compare the 3 best options for beginners:

🔹 Cashback Cards – Best for immediate everyday savings. 🔹 Travel Rewards – Best for turning spending into flights and hotels. 🔹 No Annual Fee – Best for building a rock-solid credit foundation.

Learn the professional habits needed to maximize your rewards, build your credit score, and keep your costs at zero.

Subscribe for more straightforward financial education!

#CreditCards #Finance #Beginners

segments.text: In this video, you are going to learn
how to choose the perfect credit card to
jumpstart [music] your financial
journey.
We are diving into a detailed
side-by-side comparison of three [music]
essential card types for beginners, the
cashback card for everyday value, the
travel [music] rewards card for global
adventures, and the no annual fee card
for building a rock-solid credit
foundation. [music]
You will discover exactly how to
maximize your rewards, the strategic
benefits unique to each category, and
the professional habits that ensure your
credit score thrives year after year.
We will also cover the most effective
[music] ways to manage your accounts to
keep your costs at zero while unlocking
the maximum [music] possible benefits
from the banking system. By the end of
this 8-minute educational breakdown,
[music] you will have a clear,
actionable roadmap to selecting the
specific tool that [music] fits your
lifestyle and supports your long-term
financial success.
Knowledge is the foundation of
confidence, so let's get started with
your financial education. Let us begin
with the cashback card, a tool defined
by its efficiency and immediate tangible
value.
The core philosophy of a cashback
strategy is simple.
It allows you to capture a portion of
the value from every transaction you
make.
In a typical day, you might use your
card for groceries, transportation, or
even a simple cup of coffee.
With a well-chosen cashback card, a
percentage of that expenditure is
returned directly to you.
This is not just a reward, it is a
strategic optimization of your existing
budget.
For a beginner, the beauty of cashback
lies in its transparency.
You don't need to calculate complex
point conversions or navigate travel
portals to understand the value you are
receiving. It is a direct
relationship between your spending and
your rewards. Some cards offer a flat
rate of return on everything you buy,
while others feature rotating categories
that offer even higher percentages on
things like dining or home improvements.
The key to mastering this card is
matching the reward structure to your
actual lifestyle.
By aligning your card choice with your
highest spending categories, you ensure
that your financial tool is working at
its peak efficiency, effectively giving
you a discount on the cost of living.
Beyond the basic percentage, cashback
cards often offer versatile ways to
utilize your earnings.
You can choose to apply your rewards as
a statement credit, which directly
reduces your monthly balance,
or you can have the funds deposited into
a high-yield savings account to further
your interest-earning potential. This
creates a cycle of growth where your
rewards are not just spent, but invested
back into your future.
From an educational standpoint, it is
important to remember that the most
effective way to use a cashback card is
to treat it as a tool for purchases you
were already planning to make.
When you combine this with the habit of
paying your balance in full every single
month, you are essentially participating
in a system where the bank pays you for
your loyalty and your responsible
management.
This creates a powerful incentive to
stay organized and mindful of your cash
flow.
As you become more comfortable, you
might even consider stacking rewards by
using your cashback card in conjunction
with store loyalty programs, further
magnifying the value of every dollar you
invest in your needs and wants. Now, let
us shift our focus to the travel rewards
card, a tool designed for those who view
the world as a classroom and a
destination.
These cards operate on a system of
points or miles, which can be redeemed
for flights, hotel stays, and unique
experiences that might otherwise require
significant capital. The most compelling
feature of these cards is often the
introductory bonus, a substantial reward
offered for meeting a specific spending
milestone early in your journey with the
card. For many, these bonuses provide
the foundation for their first
international flight or a luxury weekend
getaway. However, the true mastery of a
travel card comes from understanding the
ecosystem of partners.
Many top-tier cards allow you to
transfer your points to various airline
and hotel loyalty programs, often at a
rate that increases the value of those
points significantly.
This is where your financial education
pays off. Learning to navigate these
transfer partners is like learning a new
language that speaks directly to your
travel goals.
Additionally, these cards often include
auxiliary benefits like trip
cancellation insurance, rental car
coverage, and access to exclusive
airport lounges, which add layers of
security and comfort to your travels.
For many entering the world of credit,
the no annual fee beginner card is the
most logical and stable starting point.
Its primary purpose is not necessarily
high-octane rewards, but rather the
consistent and steady construction of a
healthy credit history. Because there is
no annual cost to maintain the account,
this card becomes a permanent fixture in
your financial portfolio.
In the world of credit scoring, the age
of your accounts is a critical factor,
and keeping your oldest account open and
active for decades is one of the most
effective ways to demonstrate long-term
responsibility to future lenders.
This card provides a low-pressure
environment where you can learn the
essential rhythms of credit, monitoring
your statements, understanding your
billing cycles, and ensuring your
payments are always on time.
It is a commitment to your future self,
ensuring that when the time comes to
apply for a mortgage or a car loan, you
have a long, unblemished record of
success. It is the quiet, steady engine
that powers your financial reputation,
working in the background while you
focus on your broader career and life
goals. Regardless of the card you
choose, your success is ultimately
determined by the habits you cultivate.
The most important lesson in credit
education is the power of the full
monthly payment.
By paying your entire statement balance
every month, you ensure that the cost of
using credit remains at zero. This
allows you to focus entirely on the
growth aspects, the rewards, the points,
and the credit score improvements.
Another vital concept is credit
utilization, which is the percentage of
your available credit that you are
currently using. A best practice is to
keep this number below 30 %, which
signals to the financial world that you
are managing your resources with care
and foresight.
Modern technology makes this easier than
ever.
Setting up autopay and mobile alerts
ensures that you are always in control
of your timeline.
Think of these habits not as chores, but
as the maintenance of a high-performance
vehicle.
When you take care of the mechanics, the
tool takes you exactly where you want to
go safely and efficiently. As we
conclude this guide, remember that the
right card is simply the one that best
supports your current vision. Whether
you choose the immediate value of
cashback, the global potential of travel
rewards, or the solid foundation of a no
annual fee card,
you are now equipped with the knowledge
to make that choice with confidence.
Education is the bridge between where
you are and where you want to be.
By staying informed, remaining
disciplined, and focusing on positive
growth, you are taking command of your
financial destiny. Use these tools
wisely, stay committed to your best
practices and watch as your
opportunities expand alongside your
financial expertise.
Thank you for investing this time in
your education. I am Valentino and I
look forward to seeing your financial
success flourish.

The most compelling feature of these cards is often the introductory bonus, a substantial reward offered for meeting a specific spending milestone early in your journey with the card. For many, these bonuses provide the foundation for their first international flight or a luxury weekend getaway. However, the true mastery of a travel card comes from understanding the ecosystem of partners. Many top-tier cards allow you to transfer your points to various airline and hotel loyalty programs, often at a rate that increases the value of those points significantly. This is where your financial education pays off. Learning to navigate these transfer partners is like learning a new language that speaks directly to your travel goals. Additionally, these cards often include auxiliary benefits like trip cancellation insurance, rental car coverage, and access to exclusive airport lounges, which add layers of security and comfort to your travels. For many entering the world of credit, the no annual fee beginner card is the most logical and stable starting point. Its primary purpose is not necessarily high-octane rewards, but rather the consistent and steady construction of a healthy credit history. Because there is no annual cost to maintain the account, this card becomes a permanent fixture in your financial portfolio. In the world of credit scoring, the age of your accounts is a critical factor, and keeping your oldest account open and active for decades is one of the most effective ways to demonstrate long-term responsibility to future lenders. This card provides a low-pressure environment where you can learn the essential rhythms of credit, monitoring your statements, understanding your billing cycles, and ensuring your payments are always on time. It is a commitment to your future self, ensuring that when the time comes to apply for a mortgage or a car loan, you have a long, unblemished record of success. It is the quiet, steady engine that powers your financial reputation, working in the background while you focus on your broader career and life goals. Regardless of the card you choose, your success is ultimately determined by the habits you cultivate. The most important lesson in credit education is the power of the full monthly payment. By paying your entire statement balance every month, you ensure that the cost of using credit remains at zero. This allows you to focus entirely on the growth aspects, the rewards, the points, and the credit score improvements. Another vital concept is credit utilization, which is the percentage of your available credit that you are currently using. A best practice is to keep this number below 30 %, which signals to the financial world that you are managing your resources with care and foresight. Modern technology makes this easier than ever. Setting up autopay and mobile alerts ensures that you are always in control of your timeline. Think of these habits not as chores, but as the maintenance of a high-performance vehicle. When you take care of the mechanics, the tool takes you exactly where you want to go safely and efficiently. As we conclude this guide, remember that the right card is simply the one that best supports your current vision. Whether you choose the immediate value of cashback, the global potential of travel rewards, or the solid foundation of a no annual fee card, you are now equipped with the knowledge to make that choice with confidence. Education is the bridge between where you are and where you want to be. By staying informed, remaining disciplined, and focusing on positive growth, you are taking command of your financial destiny. Use these tools wisely, stay committed to your best practices and watch as your opportunities expand alongside your financial expertise. Thank you for investing this time in your education. I am Valentino and I look forward to seeing your financial success flourish.

Capital One Spark Classic Credit Card Review 2026 | Business Credit Building Card Explained

If you’re a small business owner working on building or improving your business credit profile, this review explains how the Capital One Spark Classic Credit Card works in 2026 and why it’s often considered by newer or growing businesses. Many entrepreneurs look for a credit card that focuses on access and credit development rather than complex rewards programs, and this card is designed with that idea in mind.

The Capital One Spark Classic Credit Card is typically aimed at businesses that may not yet qualify for premium rewards cards but still want a reliable payment option for everyday expenses. Purchases such as supplies, services, travel bookings, and operational costs can be managed through one account while also helping establish payment history over time. Responsible use, such as making on-time payments and keeping balances manageable, can support credit growth.

Another reason business owners explore this card is its straightforward structure. Instead of dealing with complicated earning systems, the focus stays on usability, access to credit, and tools that help track spending across a business. This can be helpful for freelancers, startups, and small teams that want to stay organized while managing expenses.

In this review, you’ll learn how the card works, the types of benefits it offers, the fees to understand, and whether it’s the right business credit card for building credit in 2026.

Can your business really get $150,000 in business credit? Yes — but almost never from ONE card.

The average small business credit card limit is about $56,100 (Experian data) — and new businesses usually start between $5K and $50K. So $150K is a STACKING story: the right cards, at the right banks, in the right order. This video breaks down the exact stack:

🏦 BANK 1 — Chase Ink Business Preferred®
$95/yr · 3x points on travel, shipping, internet/phone & ads (first $150K of spend/yr) · 100,000 bonus points after $8,000 spend in 3 months · Apply FIRST — Chase is the strictest about recent applications

🏦 BANK 2 — Amex Business Gold ($375/yr) / Business Platinum ($895/yr)
Charge cards with NO PRESET SPENDING LIMIT — that means flexible, not unlimited. Your purchasing power adapts to your purchase, payment and credit history · 4X points in your top 2 categories

🏦 BANK 3 — Capital One Spark Cash Plus
$150/yr (refunded every year you spend $150K+) · Flat 2% cash back on everything · No preset spending limit · $2,000 bonus after $30,000 spend in 3 months

📊 PLUS: the Federal Reserve's own data on who actually gets approved — only 42% of applicants got the full amount they asked for, and small banks fully approved 57% of applicants vs 43% at large banks (Small Business Credit Survey).

metadata.title: Vivid Seats | How to Accept Electronic Ticket Transfer from Ticketmaster
metadata.author: Vivid Seats
metadata.shortDescription:
You’ve purchased tickets on Vivid Seats — great work! Whether you’re going to a concert, game, or show, we’ll help you receive electronic tickets transferred from Ticketmaster so you can enjoy your event to the fullest. This video shows you how to accept a Ticketmaster electronic ticket transfer.


TROUBLESHOOTING

0:00 - Intro
2:30 - Don’t see tickets when logged in
2:57 - Tickets not available instantly
3:17 - Error message
3:50 - Don’t see QR or barcode
4:06 - Error message with “accept tickets” button


First, you’ll get an email from Vivid Seats with a ticket delivery date and how-to email explaining where your tickets will be coming from. Since Vivid Seats is a marketplace, your seller will transfer the tickets to you. This can take a bit of time; you may not receive the tickets instantly, but they’re on their way.

Once the transfer is initiated, you’ll receive an email from Ticketmaster, the venue, or the team you bought tickets for. If you’re not seeing a transfer email in your inbox, try searching “accept tickets,” “sent you tickets” or the name of the concert, performer, stadium, or team you bought tickets to, or check your spam folder.

Once you receive the transfer email, click the accept tickets button in the email. Login with the same email you used to buy tickets on Vivid Seats and you’ll automatically see your tickets. If you don’t have an account with the site you’re on, you’ll need to create one to accept your tickets. Be sure to use the same email you used on Vivid Seats — this is key as emails must match to receive tickets.

Once you’re logged in, you’ll be prompted to accept your tickets. You’ll see a QR code, touchless tap ticket, or barcode that will be used for entry. Add your tickets to your mobile wallet for easy access at event time. As a reminder, your tickets will not be in the Vivid Seats app. Use your mobile wallet or Ticketmaster.com to access your electronic tickets at event time.


TROUBLESHOOTING TIPS:

If you click the acceptance link and you’re logged in but don’t see your tickets, triple check that the account you’re logging into has the same email as the one you used on Vivid Seats to buy your tickets. If your emails don’t match, you’ll have to make a new Ticketmaster account that matches the Vivid Seats email you used to buy your tickets. Emails must match to transfer.

Since tickets are being transferred to you by a seller, they may not be available instantly. Check your order confirmation email from Vivid Seats for expected timing and information about where they’re coming from.

If you click the accept tickets button in your email and receive the message “Oops! Something went wrong”, a 403 error, or “blocked/forbidden,” there may be connection issues. Try a different device or browser, or go into private mode. You can also wait and try again in an hour or so.

If you accept your tickets and follow the link but don’t see a barcode or QR code, your event may be too far in the future to access tickets. For security reasons, some venues will not release your ticket code for 24-48 hours before the event.

If you click the “accept tickets” button in your email and receive a “link expired” message or a similar error, it could be that your ticket acceptance link was time sensitive. Go to the site indicated in the email and log in or create an account. Your tickets may appear. Try checking the “My Tickets” or “My Events” tab.

Remember, our 100% Buyer Guarantee means your purchase is secure, your tickets are verified, and you’ll get into your event or your money back.

Need further assistance? We’re here for you! Contact Vivid Seats Customer Service via email: support@vividseats.com, Live Chat: ​​https://www.vividseats.com/vivid-seats-customer-service.html or for events in the next 24 hours, call us at ​​833.228.5143.



Vivid Seats is not affiliated with Ticketmaster or Live Nation Entertainment, Inc. (“Live Nation”).  Vivid Seats’s goods and services, including but not limited to the Vivid Seats app, are not endorsed by, directly affiliated with, maintained, authorized, or sponsored by Ticketmaster or Live Nation. So the answer would be yes. >> All right. So with this Home Depot example, we see that sometimes you're buying $50 gift cards, $100 gift cards, $500. Why is that? >> Yeah, so going back briefly to what I mentioned a minute ago about the different like levels of supply and demand for each denomination, that is going to affect the payout rate. So a lot of times there are I don't know if Home Depot is the best example, but there are some brands where you will see promos on $50 cards. So there're like Carter's for example and Adidas and Gap. I've seen those kind of deals on those brands where you might be able to buy a $50 card from somewhere for only $40. So you're getting it at 20% off. Whereas for $500 cards, it's very rare that you see any kind of promotions like that. So since there's the ability to procure those smaller denomination cards at lower rates, that's why we're able to pay lower rates because then that ends up also affecting the demand on the selling side cuz I mean it's a competitive market. So, what that ends up meaning is that we're able to sell those at a lower price on the selling side as well. In addition to that, a lot of customers who do arbitrage, especially if they're doing bulk and they're buying lots of gift cards for their business, they many times will prefer to buy the higher denomination cards because for example, if they're going to spend $50,000 at some retailer buying products to resell, they're probably going to want to use $500 cards just so they have less to manage. They don't only have 100 cards in total as opposed to 1,000. And for that reason, a lot of times those customers are willing to pay higher rates for higher denomination cards. That makes sense. All right, so what's the difference between just like rates, reservations, deals, what's the gift card section? So, the gift card section shows you the actual gift cards that you have submitted to us. So, it just basically gives you the full history of the cards that you've sent us. How fast does somebody find out if something was denied? Like if you accidentally type in a number wrong, how fast is that turnaround time? So, for us it's fairly quick. I would say normally within one to two business days and only two business days if we have like a huge backlog of cards that we're still working through in terms of balance checking, but since we balance check each card as we receive them before we sell them to customers, that allows us to let people know a lot quicker if there's any issues with the cards they submit than we would be able to otherwise if we're just selling cards to our end buyers without checking that. Now, there are scenarios where like a card could be good when we receive it and when we check it and then later on due to some fluke reason like it's deactivated by the retailer or if it's a compromised card and the money was drained on it, things like that can happen where we might have to come back and ask the supplier to help us resolve it later on. And there's also times where with certain brands you just can't balance check them online at all. So, we can't really do that in those cases, but yeah, that's what that's normally with the time frame that we're looking at. >> What are some of your favorite deals for finding like discounted gift cards or where you stack them with different Amex offers? What are some of the best ones where you're just like, "Guys, you should jump on this whenever it comes up." >> That's a good question. I don't know if if this is the best example, but one that comes to mind is when there are Tory Burch Amex offers because those normally are 20% back in the form of statement credits. So, you'd buy a a $300 Tory Burch gift card and get $60 back. And normally we're able to pay around like 85 to 87% historically for those cards. So, it's fairly profitable on each card if you just look at the the actual profit margin. And then it's just a matter of scaling up and doing as much volume with that as you can since normally only one offer per card, but obviously you can use card pointers and things like that to try to do a little bit more volume. I mean, there's risk of Amex clawing back points, there's risk of shutdown from different issuers whether it be Chase, Citi, Capital One, whoever. And there's even times where you run into obstacles where for example, you're trying to buy gift cards at a physical store and they don't want to let you, whatever retailer maybe they decide that they only want to let you buy with cash or only debit card or things like that or especially if you go in multiple times and try to scale something up they might not like it. So, the risk is always there. I would say operate within your own risk tolerance. I think that's the general rule of thumb when it comes to gift card selling and if you have any other thoughts Julia, feel free to chime in here as well. But but yeah, there's always some risk. There's also risk of compromised cards if you buy cards at a grocery store and some like scammer has gone in there and tampered with them and then somehow gets as the card numbers and is waiting to use it once you activate it. So, there's definitely things that can happen but I think people just have to be aware of that and start out small. You like network with other people in this world who do the same thing and yeah, just don't get in over your head too much. I agree with all of that. I also highly encourage people not to like be so dependent on one play. So much of just the points and miles ecosystem and strategy is knowing that there's a lot of different angles that you can approach this from. I always tell people please please please put real money in front of points money. Prioritize your actual financial health cuz there's so many people where they're just like dependent on one play like the Alaska Safeway thing that no longer exists outside of Alaska or way back in the day when there was that US Mint thing where you could buy gold coins it was like a dollar gold coin and you could buy it for a dollar and then just ship that coin in a wheelbarrow over to your bank and people were just like you churned through it and then people freaked out when other people found out that it was a thing. I think there is something to be said for accepting the fact that everything in this world of points and miles that we play in could be very temporary and we enjoy it while it exists. Try not to burn it to the ground but more so try not to burn your personal finance to the ground in pursuit of these things. Always prioritize your financial health before you go into something like this. But tell us a little bit about the WhatsApp groups, the Telegram groups. If somebody wants to get in on all of what you do at QCGC, where is the best place to do that? Yeah, so you can sign up at qcgc.io. Just click the one of the various sign up buttons that are there. And once you create an account, you will receive an automated welcome email that contains both the onboarding course to show you how to get started. You can go through some of those guides and learn about how everything works. And it also includes the links to both of our Telegram channels, one of which is the deals channel where we send out deals. Now, we also send them out via email, like every single deal we send out via email. And we're also adding SMS text messaging in there, too, if you want to get the alerts via text message. But yeah, so the links to the Telegram channels will be in there, both the deals channel and the group chat, which is good. So, you can actually talk to other group members as well. And if you're new and want to go in there and ask people what their experience has been. Like if you're feeling kind of unsure, hesitant about it, you can take advantage of that and communicate with those other users. >> Perfect. Well, thank you again, Taylor, so much for joining us once again on the GeoBreeze Travel Podcast. And I look forward to hearing from everyone on what they think of QCGC. All right. Thank you, Julia. Appreciate it.

metadata.author: Ash Automates
metadata.shortDescription:
➡️ Sign up to Connect: https://www.connect-tickets.com/

Selling tickets across multiple marketplaces creates one major problem: the same inventory can still be live on several sites after it sells somewhere else.

In this video, I break down how Connect helps professional ticket sellers manage inventory across multiple marketplaces from one place, reduce oversells, sync pricing, handle fulfillment, reconcile payouts, and understand which sales channels are actually performing.

Connect is not another ticket marketplace. It connects to your existing seller accounts so your marketplace relationships, account history, and payouts remain yours while Connect becomes the operational layer underneath them.

You'll see how Connect Core keeps inventory synchronized in real time, how its Seller API works with existing inventory systems, how pricing and Market Intelligence work, and how orders, fulfillment, finance, analytics, B2B inventory, and direct sales fit into the same platform.

Connect makes the most sense for professional ticket sellers and brokers managing inventory across several resale marketplaces. If you're only selling the occasional pair of tickets, it's probably more infrastructure than you need.

Connect partnered with us on this video.

segments.text: # How to Sell Tickets on Multiple Marketplaces Without Overselling
If you sell tickets on more than one marketplace, you've probably had this happen many times. A
pair sells on one site, and until you notice, the same pair is still for sale on the others.
If someone buys them there first, you've sold tickets that you don't have anymore.
Marketplaces like StubHub charge sellers for orders that they can't fulfill,
and that can include the cost of replacement tickets,
which for a sold-out event can be more than you sold the originals for.
Connect is an AI-driven ticketing platform built to stop that from happening,
and it covers a lot more than that one problem.
In this review, I'll go through what Connect actually is, how it keeps your
inventory in sync across marketplaces, what it does for pricing, fulfillment,
and your finances, what it costs, and who it's genuinely worth it for.
If you'd like to check out Connect as you watch along,
go ahead and get started using the link below this video at your convenience.
Now, let's get right into it.
## What Connect Is
If you're completely unfamiliar, the simplest way to describe Connect is
that it sits underneath your ticket business rather than on top of it.
It's not a marketplace on its own, and it doesn't sell tickets under its own name.
Instead, it connects to your own seller accounts on each marketplace and becomes
the one place where your inventory, pricing, orders, and money are managed.
Connect's own pitch is "list once, sell everywhere."
The idea behind it is simple. Your tickets get entered in one place,
and every marketplace you sell on reads from that record instead of keeping its own separate copy.
That one change is one of the main things you're paying for,
so it's worth understanding why it matters.
## How Connect Stops Oversells
When you list by hand, every marketplace holds its own version of your inventory.
Five marketplaces means five copies of the truth, and you're the one keeping them in agreement.
A sale on one site doesn't touch the other four until you log in and take
that listing down. That delay is exactly where overselling happens.
Connect replaces that with what it calls Connect Core:
a single inventory record that syncs to your connected marketplaces in real time.
When a ticket sells, that change comes from that one record,
so availability updates across every channel without you chasing it from tab to tab.
The same goes for price changes. You edit a price once and it goes out everywhere
instead of leaving one listing stuck at an old price that buyers skip right past.
Getting inventory in works two ways.
You can create listings directly in Connect, which is what you see right here.
Or, if you already run a POS, an internal tool, or even a spreadsheet,
Connect's Seller API lets you push inventory from that system into Connect as it changes.
API access comes at no extra cost,
and Connect says it handles thousands of listings across dozens of events.
For a broker with an established setup, that matters because you keep your
existing system and Connect becomes the layer that distributes from it.
## Your Marketplace Accounts Stay Yours
One of the most important points, in my opinion,
and exactly why I recommend Connect over a lot of alternatives, is that your accounts stay yours.
It's one of the biggest differentiators.
Because Connect links to each marketplace through
your own seller account and your own API key, your account history,
your standing, and your relationship with each marketplace all stay in your name.
The marketplace pays you directly.
Connect's terms are explicit that it isn't the merchant of record on
those sales and that payouts from marketplaces go straight to you.
Compare that with consignment, where a service sells your tickets through
its own account and pays you once it's been paid.
Consignment can be easier to start with, and for some sellers that's the right trade.
But you give up a lot of control over where your tickets go,
your marketplace relationships, and a clear view of your own money.
Connect, on the other hand, is built for sellers who want the reach without giving those things up.
It works with a mix of US, European, and international resale marketplaces,
and the exact channels available depend on your account and market.
You also pick which channels each ticket group goes to.
A high-demand fixture can go everywhere,
while something with a local audience stays on the channels that actually have buyers for it.
And if you don't have an account on a marketplace yet, Connect's team can help you set one up.
## Pricing and Market Intelligence
Let's move on to pricing and market data.
Pricing in Connect works on two levels.
You can change prices yourself and have them apply across every channel at once, or you can
set pricing rules that adjust automatically based on live demand and performance data.
Alongside that is Market Intelligence, which shows demand trends and what competitors are
asking across channels, so your decisions are based on what the market is actually doing.
One detail I appreciate is that Connect is clear that the rules are yours.
Its terms say the automated pricing rules are configured
by you and that it doesn't guarantee revenue outcomes.
It carries out your strategy rather than replacing it with one you don't understand,
and that's the right way around for a professional seller.
## Orders and Fulfillment
Preventing the double sale is half of it.
The buyer who did get the tickets still has to receive them.
Orders from every connected marketplace land in one Orders view,
so you work from a single queue instead of checking a different dashboard for each site.
You open an order, go to Ticket Fulfillment, and deliver the tickets from there.
If you delivered them some other way, you upload proof of delivery so the record stays complete.
## Finance, Reconciliation, and Analytics
Now let's talk about the part that can save you the most time and money.
Once tickets are delivered, you still need to know what each sale was invoiced at,
what the marketplace actually paid after its fees, and whether those numbers match your books.
Across hundreds of orders from several marketplaces,
that turns into a spreadsheet nobody wants to open.
Connect's Finance Hub reconciles invoices, payouts, and payments
across every connected marketplace and your private sales in one place.
It also connects directly to Xero,
so your accounting is built from the same data as your sales.
On top of that, Connect's analytics show which channels actually move your inventory,
at what price, and how fast.
There's also a B2B layer for trading inventory with sellers you trust
and a branded storefront for selling directly to buyers under your own name.
## What Connect Costs
If you're wondering how much Connect actually costs,
it charges a percentage of the revenue that goes through the platform, invoiced monthly.
Because the marketplaces pay you directly, that fee never comes out of your payouts.
It arrives as its own invoice.
## Who Connect Is For
So who is Connect actually for?
If you only sell the occasional pair of tickets,
Connect is more than what you need. You can list them on one site and be done.
But if you're running several events across a handful of marketplaces, this is where it starts
to earn its keep, because every sale you currently manage by hand is another opportunity to oversell.
And if you're a full operation with your own inventory system, staff, and books,
the API, market data, and finance side become even bigger reasons to use it.
## Final Verdict
In conclusion, Connect does what it sets out to do.
It gives you one record of your inventory that every marketplace reads from, which is
the actual fix for overselling, and it builds the rest of the operation around that record:
pricing, orders, fulfillment, reconciliation, and analytics.
What makes it stand out further is how it does that.
Your accounts, your marketplace relationships,
and your payouts all stay yours, which matters more the bigger your business gets.
If you're currently selling across multiple marketplaces
and still keeping them in sync by hand, it's well worth a look.
You'll find the link to Connect in the description and below this video
in the comments, and their team will help you connect the marketplaces you already sell on.
Thanks so much for watching this video. If you found it helpful or informative,
let me know by giving it a thumbs up, and make sure to subscribe to
the channel so you don't miss any follow-up content similar to this.

Connect is an AI-driven ticketing platform built to stop that from happening, and it covers a lot more than that one problem. In this review, I'll go through what Connect actually is, how it keeps your inventory in sync across marketplaces, what it does for pricing, fulfillment, and your finances, what it costs, and who it's genuinely worth it for. If you'd like to check out Connect as you watch along, go ahead and get started using the link below this video at your convenience. Now, let's get right into it. ## What Connect Is If you're completely unfamiliar, the simplest way to describe Connect is that it sits underneath your ticket business rather than on top of it. It's not a marketplace on its own, and it doesn't sell tickets under its own name. Instead, it connects to your own seller accounts on each marketplace and becomes the one place where your inventory, pricing, orders, and money are managed. Connect's own pitch is "list once, sell everywhere." The idea behind it is simple. Your tickets get entered in one place, and every marketplace you sell on reads from that record instead of keeping its own separate copy. That one change is one of the main things you're paying for, so it's worth understanding why it matters. ## How Connect Stops Oversells When you list by hand, every marketplace holds its own version of your inventory. Five marketplaces means five copies of the truth, and you're the one keeping them in agreement. A sale on one site doesn't touch the other four until you log in and take that listing down. That delay is exactly where overselling happens. Connect replaces that with what it calls Connect Core: a single inventory record that syncs to your connected marketplaces in real time. When a ticket sells, that change comes from that one record, so availability updates across every channel without you chasing it from tab to tab. The same goes for price changes. You edit a price once and it goes out everywhere instead of leaving one listing stuck at an old price that buyers skip right past. Getting inventory in works two ways. You can create listings directly in Connect, which is what you see right here. Or, if you already run a POS, an internal tool, or even a spreadsheet, Connect's Seller API lets you push inventory from that system into Connect as it changes. API access comes at no extra cost, and Connect says it handles thousands of listings across dozens of events. For a broker with an established setup, that matters because you keep your existing system and Connect becomes the layer that distributes from it. ## Your Marketplace Accounts Stay Yours One of the most important points, in my opinion, and exactly why I recommend Connect over a lot of alternatives, is that your accounts stay yours. It's one of the biggest differentiators. Because Connect links to each marketplace through your own seller account and your own API key, your account history, your standing, and your relationship with each marketplace all stay in your name. The marketplace pays you directly. Connect's terms are explicit that it isn't the merchant of record on those sales and that payouts from marketplaces go straight to you. Compare that with consignment, where a service sells your tickets through its own account and pays you once it's been paid. Consignment can be easier to start with, and for some sellers that's the right trade. But you give up a lot of control over where your tickets go, your marketplace relationships, and a clear view of your own money. Connect, on the other hand, is built for sellers who want the reach without giving those things up. It works with a mix of US, European, and international resale marketplaces, and the exact channels available depend on your account and market. You also pick which channels each ticket group goes to. A high-demand fixture can go everywhere, while something with a local audience stays on the channels that actually have buyers for it. And if you don't have an account on a marketplace yet, Connect's team can help you set one up. ## Pricing and Market Intelligence Let's move on to pricing and market data. Pricing in Connect works on two levels. You can change prices yourself and have them apply across every channel at once, or you can set pricing rules that adjust automatically based on live demand and performance data. Alongside that is Market Intelligence, which shows demand trends and what competitors are asking across channels, so your decisions are based on what the market is actually doing. One detail I appreciate is that Connect is clear that the rules are yours. Its terms say the automated pricing rules are configured by you and that it doesn't guarantee revenue outcomes. It carries out your strategy rather than replacing it with one you don't understand, and that's the right way around for a professional seller. ## Orders and Fulfillment Preventing the double sale is half of it. The buyer who did get the tickets still has to receive them. Orders from every connected marketplace land in one Orders view, so you work from a single queue instead of checking a different dashboard for each site. You open an order, go to Ticket Fulfillment, and deliver the tickets from there. If you delivered them some other way, you upload proof of delivery so the record stays complete. ## Finance, Reconciliation, and Analytics Now let's talk about the part that can save you the most time and money. Once tickets are delivered, you still need to know what each sale was invoiced at, what the marketplace actually paid after its fees, and whether those numbers match your books. Across hundreds of orders from several marketplaces, that turns into a spreadsheet nobody wants to open. Connect's Finance Hub reconciles invoices, payouts, and payments across every connected marketplace and your private sales in one place. It also connects directly to Xero, so your accounting is built from the same data as your sales. On top of that, Connect's analytics show which channels actually move your inventory, at what price, and how fast. There's also a B2B layer for trading inventory with sellers you trust and a branded storefront for selling directly to buyers under your own name. ## What Connect Costs If you're wondering how much Connect actually costs, it charges a percentage of the revenue that goes through the platform, invoiced monthly. Because the marketplaces pay you directly, that fee never comes out of your payouts. It arrives as its own invoice. ## Who Connect Is For So who is Connect actually for? If you only sell the occasional pair of tickets, Connect is more than what you need. You can list them on one site and be done. But if you're running several events across a handful of marketplaces, this is where it starts to earn its keep, because every sale you currently manage by hand is another opportunity to oversell. And if you're a full operation with your own inventory system, staff, and books, the API, market data, and finance side become even bigger reasons to use it. ## Final Verdict In conclusion, Connect does what it sets out to do. It gives you one record of your inventory that every marketplace reads from, which is the actual fix for overselling, and it builds the rest of the operation around that record: pricing, orders, fulfillment, reconciliation, and analytics. What makes it stand out further is how it does that. Your accounts, your marketplace relationships, and your payouts all stay yours, which matters more the bigger your business gets. If you're currently selling across multiple marketplaces and still keeping them in sync by hand, it's well worth a look. You'll find the link to Connect in the description and below this video in the comments, and their team will help you connect the marketplaces you already sell on. Thanks so much for watching this video. If you found it helpful or informative, let me know by giving it a thumbs up, and make sure to subscribe to the channel so you don't miss any follow-up content similar to this.

With some of the biggest concerts of all time happening last year with Taylor Swift and Beyonce, it had me thinking if this was a big opportunity to make money reselling/ flipping concert tickets for a profit. You have a landlord, a contractor, or a vendor that tell you that they can only accept checks or bank transfers, no cards. Now, this is frustrating especially when you have a card sitting with a big limit and 0% interest just waiting to be used. This is where a service like Melio comes in. Melio lets you pay almost any bill with your credit card even when the person on the other side only takes checks or a bank transfer. So, here's how it works. You pay Melio with your card, then Melio sends them a check or a transfer. So, you can pay your rent, your suppliers, your contractors, even some taxes all on your credit card. The fee is usually around 2.9% and if you're chasing a sign-up bonus, that spend can pay for itself. There's one more hidden benefit and it is big for cash flow. Float. When you pay a bill with your card, you don't owe that money until your statement cycle is due. Stacking your billing cycle with your grace period, you can get 30, 40, even 50 days before you pay it back. That is free breathing room for your business. So, Melio doesn't hand you cash directly, but it does free up the cash that you already have by letting your card cover the bills. But, there is another way to do this that almost nobody on YouTube talks about. I have used this myself to hit sign-up bonuses and once you see how it works, you'll understand why most people are keeping it quiet. Before I explain this, you have probably seen other videos push manufacturer spending, buying gift cards and turning them to money orders, or buying something expensive and returning it for a refund on a different card. metadata.title: How Credit Card Companies Make Money From You (Even If You Pay in Full)
metadata.author: Mogulnomics
metadata.shortDescription:
Dave pays his credit card in full every month. Zero interest. He thinks he's beating the system. But the bank still made money on every single coffee he bought, and the guy behind him paying cash paid for Dave's rewards. Here's exactly how credit card companies make money: the swipe fee you never see, who really pays for your points, the $160 billion interest machine, the fee buffet, and the one habit that flips the game.

⏱️ Chapters
0:00 You paid in full. They still won.
0:38 The 2% you never see
2:01 Everyone pays
2:58 The rewards trick
4:16 The interest machine
6:02 The fee buffet
7:10 Why they still love Dave
7:57 The 2026 fight
8:56 How to flip the game

Watch next: Airlines Are Secretly Credit Card Companies ▶ https://youtu.be/rOsAb-eON3I
Dave's first story: How Costco Makes Money Selling $1.50 Hot Dogs

📚 Sources: Nilson Report via Merchants Payments Coalition, Visa fiscal 2026 results, Boston Fed (2010), Federal Reserve FEDS 2023-007, CFPB (2024–2025), NY Fed Household Debt (Q3 2026), Fed G.19, Bankrate (2026), Congress.gov S.3623, PYMNTS, NPR, Adobe (2026).

🔔 Subscribe for animated business breakdowns: https://www.youtube.com/@Mogulnomics?sub_confirmation=1

Education and entertainment only, not financial advice. Characters are fictional cartoons; companies are named only with reported facts.

metadata.title: Why Nobody Talks About the Credit Card Float (And How It's Making Some People Rich)
metadata.author: The Wealth Paradox
metadata.shortDescription:
Most people using credit cards think they're in control of their money. They're not — they're living on next month's income and don't know it.

This video breaks down the credit card float trap, why it feels completely normal until one financial shock hits, and the one move that breaks the cycle for good: building a one-month buffer so you're always spending money you already have, never money you haven't earned yet.

Timestamps:
00:00 - Why Living on Next Month's Income Feels Normal Until It Destroys You
03:02 - The One-Month Buffer That Breaks the Credit Card Float Forever
06:03 - How Seeing Every Dollar as a Worker Ends the Float Trap
09:03 - The Hidden Price of Every Dollar You Spend Before You Earn It
12:06 - Why Choosing Enjoyment on Purpose Is the Only Way to Stay Ahead

videos.full_text: Here is the uncomfortable truth about credit card float. Living on next month's income feels normal until one shock hits and most people do not notice until the damage has already become normal. It does not feel dramatic in the moment. It feels like a small payment, a reasonable upgrade, a harmless delay, or a smart choice that everyone around you seems to be making. But money rarely leaves your life in one giant obvious mistake. It leaks out through systems you never questioned. In this video, I am going to show you how credit card float really works, why it quietly separates people who build wealth from people who only earn money, and how to use a simple rule, break the float with a one-month buffer. If you are a salary earner, business owner, beginner investor, or someone trying to finally get ahead, this lesson can change the way you see every dollar that comes through your hands. The hidden mechanism. The first thing to understand is that credit card float is not really about one isolated decision. It is about a pattern. Living on next month's income feels normal until one shock hits, then the pattern repeats until it feels normal. A person can earn more, work harder, and still feel stuck because the system around the money never changed. That is why this matters. Wealth is not built only by finding a higher income. Wealth is built by designing a life where money has fewer places to escape before it can become ownership. Imagine two men with the same paycheck. One waits until the end of the month to see what is left. The other decides before the month begins where the important dollars will go. The difference looks small during week one, but it becomes enormous over years. The first man is constantly reacting. The second man is quietly building a machine. The credit card float nobody talks about is really a lesson about that machine because the people who win with money rarely rely on motivation. They rely on defaults. The reason smart people miss this is that the trap usually sounds reasonable. Nobody wakes up and says, "I would like to sabotage my future today." They say, "I deserve this. I can afford the payment. I will fix it next month, or I will start investing after things calm down." Those sentences feel harmless because they contain a little truth. The problem is that a little truth can still lead to a bad financial structure when it gets repeated for years. Wealthy people tend to ask a different question. They do not only ask, "Can I afford this today?" They ask, "What is this decision do to my options 5 years from now?" That question changes everything. It turns a purchase into a trade-off. It turns a tax rule into a strategy. It turns an account balance into a tool. When you use that question consistently, you start seeing the gap between looking successful and becoming financially strong. For regular investors, the goal is not to copy billionaires or pretend that every advanced strategy applies to a normal household. The goal is to use the same underlying principle at your scale. Break the float with a 1-month buffer. That may sound simple, but simple is exactly the point. The most powerful money systems are usually boring enough to repeat. If the strategy requires constant excitement, constant discipline, or constant prediction, it is fragile. A durable system should keep working on an ordinary Tuesday. The first practical move is to slow the decision down and put numbers around it. Write the monthly cost, the annual cost, and the 10-year cost. Then compare that number to what the same dollars could do if they paid down debt, filled a cash buffer, or bought a broad investment fund. You are not doing this to shame yourself. You are doing it to see clearly. Clear math turns vague stress into a decision you can actually control. The second move is to automate the part of the plan that matters most. If you wait to feel ready, the money will usually find another job. Automation removes the debate. It can be a transfer to savings, a retirement contribution, an extra debt payment, or a separate account for irregular expenses. The exact tool depends on your situation, but the principle stays the same. Important money should move before casual spending has a chance to claim it. Here is the mistake to avoid. Do not turn this into an all-or-nothing identity test. People fail financially when they believe one imperfect month means the whole plan is broken. A strong money system expects real life. It expects repairs, family needs, medical bills, holidays, and bad moods. The goal is not perfection. The goal is recovery speed. If your system helps you return to the plan quickly, it is working. A simple weekly system is enough for most people. Pick one day, open the accounts, and ask four questions. What came in? What went out? What is due soon? What needs to move before I spend it? That review can take 15 minutes. It is not glamorous, but it gives your money a manager. Without that review, your financial life is managed by due dates, advertising, social pressure, and whatever feels urgent at the moment. Over time, the payoff becomes bigger than the dollars. You begin to feel less reactive. You stop being surprised by bills that were never really surprises. You see which habits are helping and which ones are quietly taxing your future. Then the same income starts producing a different life. That is the part most people underestimate. Financial peace often begins before you become rich because peace comes from control, clarity, and direction. The mindset shift is this, every dollar is a worker and every worker needs a job. Some dollars protect you. Some dollars buy back time. Some dollars buy assets. Some dollars buy joy. The danger is not spending money. The danger is spending without knowing which future you traded away. Once you see money that way, credit card float stops being a random topic and becomes a lens for understanding your entire financial life. So here is the challenge. Before you make the next financial decision connected to credit card float, pause and ask what the decision does to your freedom. Does it create flexibility or does it create another obligation? Does it lower stress or does it hide stress behind a payment? Does it move you toward ownership or just toward the appearance of success? You do not need a perfect answer today. You only need a better question repeated long enough to change the outcome. Now let me make this practical with a simple framework. Step one is awareness. Name the money pattern without judging yourself. Step two is separation. Move the important dollars away from the spending account before they become available. Step three is automation. Make the good decision happen on schedule. Step four is review. Check the system weekly and adjust without drama. Step five is patience. Let repeated small actions become large results. That is how normal people build uncommon financial outcomes. This is educational, not personal, financial, or tax advice. Your exact choices should depend on your income, debts, family needs, risk tolerance, account options, and local rules. But the principle is universal. If you want more freedom, you need more than income. You need a system that protects income from randomness, pressure, and short-term emotion. Start with one action today, make it automatic, and let the next 12 months prove that your money can behave differently when you give it a better structure. segments.text: For businesses spending 50,000, 100,000,
or even several hundred thousand dollars
per month on inventory, advertising,
software, logistics, and other operating
expenses, choosing the right business
card can materially affect the rewards
generated from spending the company
already needs to make. At this scale,
the decision is not primarily about
airport lounge access or lifestyle
perks. It is about matching the card's
earning structure, payment requirements,
purchasing capacity, travel benefits,
and redemption options to the company's
actual spending profile.
Two premium options frequently
considered are the Capital One Venture X
Business and the American Express
Business Platinum Card. But comparing
them requires more than looking at
headline point values. You need to
understand how each card handles large
spending, which purchases earn elevated
rewards, how the payment structure
affects cash flow, and how efficiently
the rewards can ultimately be redeemed.
Let's start with purchasing capacity.
The American Express Business Platinum
operates differently from a conventional
credit card with a simple fixed credit
limit. It can offer flexible spending
capacity that adapts based on factors
considered by the issuer. But the phrase
no preset spending limit should never be
interpreted as unlimited spending.
Purchasing capacity can vary, and
individual transactions may still be
declined. Businesses planning an
unusually large purchase should
therefore verify available spending
capacity rather than assuming every
transaction will automatically be
approved. This structure can still be
useful for businesses with variable
operating expenses. A company might have
relatively normal spending one month and
then need to purchase a large amount of
inventory or equipment the next. The
Capital One Venture X Business also
needs to be evaluated according to its
current payment and spending terms.
Rather than assuming that either card
provides unlimited corporate financing,
business owners should understand the
actual spending capacity assigned to
their account and when the balance must
be paid. This is particularly important
because rewards cards should not be
confused with working capital
facilities. If your company needs to
finance inventory for several months, a
business line of credit or another
financing product may be more
appropriate than relying on a premium
rewards card.
Now, let's examine the earning
structures. This is where the two cards
can produce substantially different
results depending on how your company
spends money. The Venture X Business is
particularly attractive for businesses
that value a strong flat earning rate on
eligible everyday purchases. A flat rate
structure can be useful when spending is
fragmented across categories that do not
receive special bonuses elsewhere.
Consider a company paying for software
subscriptions, professional services,
shipping, equipment, advertising, and
miscellaneous operating expenses. If
those transactions qualify for the
card's standard earning rate, the
business can accumulate rewards without
having to constantly optimize individual
categories.
The Business Platinum takes a different
approach. American Express has offered
elevated earning opportunities on
certain eligible purchases and business
categories, subject to specific terms
and annual limits. Those categories and
thresholds can change, so businesses
should verify the current earning rules
before calculating expected annual
rewards. This is especially important
when comparing the cards using millions
of dollars of hypothetical spending. A
spending cap can dramatically change the
result. For example, an elevated
multiplier might look superior on the
first portion of eligible annual
spending, but become less competitive
after the applicable cap has been
reached. The correct comparison
therefore requires transaction level
analysis. Export 12 months of company
card activity. Separate the transactions
by category and transaction size. Then,
calculate how those same purchases would
earn under each card's current rules.
This will produce a far more useful
answer than simply declaring one card
the universal winner. Welcome offers
deserve the same discipline. Premium
business cards can periodically offer
substantial introductory bonuses after
meeting a specified spending requirement
within a limited period. But, those
offers can change and may differ
depending on the applicant, application
channel, or promotion. Never restructure
your company's purchasing solely to hit
a welcome bonus. Instead, time an
application around legitimate business
expenses you were already planning.
Inventory purchases, annual software
renewals, equipment, eligible tax
payments where economically sensible, or
other normal operating costs may help
satisfy a spending requirement
naturally. But, transaction fees must
always be considered. Paying a large
processing fee simply to earn additional
points can eliminate much of the
economic value of the bonus. And
carrying unnecessary debt to earn
rewards is an even worse trade.
The next question is redemption.
Generating hundreds of thousands or
millions of points sounds impressive,
but the real economic value depends on
what the business eventually does with
them.
American Express Membership Rewards
provide several redemption methods,
including eligible travel bookings and
transfers to participating airline and
hotel loyalty programs. The Business
Platinum may also provide a pay with
points rebate on qualifying airfare
booked through the applicable American
Express travel channel, subject to the
current benefit terms, eligible airline
rules, annual rebate limits, and other
restrictions. That can be useful for
businesses that want greater
predictability than traditional airline
award availability provides. But,
transfer partners can sometimes create
higher potential value. Instead of
redeeming points at a fixed rate,
businesses can transfer eligible rewards
into participating airline programs and
book award travel. Capital One also
provides access to travel redemptions
and participating transfer partners.
Depending on the current program, miles
can potentially be used toward eligible
travel purchases or transferred into
participating airline and hotel loyalty
programs. For both ecosystems, transfer
partners create opportunities, but also
introduce complexity. Award availability
can disappear. Airlines can change award
pricing. Taxes and surcharges can be
substantial, and transferring points
into an airline program is generally not
something you should do without a
specific redemption strategy. Once
transferable points have been moved into
an external loyalty program, reversing
that transfer may not be possible. For
executive travel, the strongest strategy
is often to search for the flight first,
determine the cash price, determine the
award price, calculate the effective
value per point, then transfer only the
points required for the booking.
There is another issue that
high-spending businesses should not
ignore. Operational resilience. If
millions of dollars in annual expenses
are being routed through one card
ecosystem, a temporary fraud review,
transaction decline, account
restriction, or payment processing
problem could disrupt company
operations. A sophisticated corporate
card strategy, therefore, should not
depend entirely on a single payment
instrument. Businesses with substantial
operating expenses may benefit from
maintaining multiple payment methods and
allocating spending according to the
strengths of each. That can also change
the Venture X Business versus Business
Platinum question. For some companies,
the correct answer may not be choosing
one and eliminating the other. It may be
using each card selectively. A flat-rate
card can handle eligible general
operating expenses. Another card can be
used when its category bonuses, travel
benefits, purchasing capacity, or
redemption features create greater
value. But, rewards should remain
secondary to financial controls. Your
accounting team needs clean
reconciliation. Employee cards need
appropriate controls. Fraud monitoring
needs to be effective. Cash must be
available when payments are due. And
card usage should integrate cleanly with
the company's expense management and
accounting systems. A 2% rewards
difference means very little if poor
treasury management creates interest,
late fees, cash flow problems, or
accounting complexity.
So, which card is better? The Capital
One Venture X Business can be compelling
for businesses that prioritize a
straightforward earning structure on
broad eligible spending and value the
Capital One travel ecosystem. The
American Express Business Platinum can
be compelling for companies that can
extract meaningful value from its
current bonus categories, premium travel

videos.full_text: For businesses spending 50,000, 100,000, or even several hundred thousand dollars per month on inventory, advertising, software, logistics, and other operating expenses, choosing the right business card can materially affect the rewards generated from spending the company already needs to make. At this scale, the decision is not primarily about airport lounge access or lifestyle perks. It is about matching the card's earning structure, payment requirements, purchasing capacity, travel benefits, and redemption options to the company's actual spending profile. Two premium options frequently considered are the Capital One Venture X Business and the American Express Business Platinum Card. But comparing them requires more than looking at headline point values. You need to understand how each card handles large spending, which purchases earn elevated rewards, how the payment structure affects cash flow, and how efficiently the rewards can ultimately be redeemed. Let's start with purchasing capacity. The American Express Business Platinum operates differently from a conventional credit card with a simple fixed credit limit. It can offer flexible spending capacity that adapts based on factors considered by the issuer. But the phrase no preset spending limit should never be interpreted as unlimited spending. Purchasing capacity can vary, and individual transactions may still be declined. Businesses planning an unusually large purchase should therefore verify available spending capacity rather than assuming every transaction will automatically be approved. This structure can still be useful for businesses with variable operating expenses. A company might have relatively normal spending one month and then need to purchase a large amount of inventory or equipment the next. The Capital One Venture X Business also needs to be evaluated according to its current payment and spending terms. Rather than assuming that either card provides unlimited corporate financing, business owners should understand the actual spending capacity assigned to their account and when the balance must be paid. This is particularly important because rewards cards should not be confused with working capital facilities. If your company needs to finance inventory for several months, a business line of credit or another financing product may be more appropriate than relying on a premium rewards card. Now, let's examine the earning structures. This is where the two cards can produce substantially different results depending on how your company spends money. The Venture X Business is particularly attractive for businesses that value a strong flat earning rate on eligible everyday purchases. A flat rate structure can be useful when spending is fragmented across categories that do not receive special bonuses elsewhere. Consider a company paying for software subscriptions, professional services, shipping, equipment, advertising, and miscellaneous operating expenses. If those transactions qualify for the card's standard earning rate, the business can accumulate rewards without having to constantly optimize individual categories. The Business Platinum takes a different approach. American Express has offered elevated earning opportunities on certain eligible purchases and business categories, subject to specific terms and annual limits. Those categories and thresholds can change, so businesses should verify the current earning rules before calculating expected annual rewards. This is especially important when comparing the cards using millions of dollars of hypothetical spending. A spending cap can dramatically change the result. For example, an elevated multiplier might look superior on the first portion of eligible annual spending, but become less competitive after the applicable cap has been reached. The correct comparison therefore requires transaction level analysis. Export 12 months of company card activity. Separate the transactions by category and transaction size. Then, calculate how those same purchases would earn under each card's current rules. This will produce a far more useful answer than simply declaring one card the universal winner. Welcome offers deserve the same discipline. Premium business cards can periodically offer substantial introductory bonuses after meeting a specified spending requirement within a limited period. But, those offers can change and may differ depending on the applicant, application channel, or promotion. Never restructure your company's purchasing solely to hit a welcome bonus. Instead, time an application around legitimate business expenses you were already planning. Inventory purchases, annual software renewals, equipment, eligible tax payments where economically sensible, or other normal operating costs may help satisfy a spending requirement naturally. But, transaction fees must always be considered. Paying a large processing fee simply to earn additional points can eliminate much of the economic value of the bonus. And carrying unnecessary debt to earn rewards is an even worse trade. The next question is redemption. Generating hundreds of thousands or millions of points sounds impressive, but the real economic value depends on what the business eventually does with them. American Express Membership Rewards provide several redemption methods, including eligible travel bookings and transfers to participating airline and hotel loyalty programs. The Business Platinum may also provide a pay with points rebate on qualifying airfare booked through the applicable American Express travel channel, subject to the current benefit terms, eligible airline rules, annual rebate limits, and other restrictions. That can be useful for businesses that want greater predictability than traditional airline award availability provides. But, transfer partners can sometimes create higher potential value. Instead of redeeming points at a fixed rate, businesses can transfer eligible rewards into participating airline programs and book award travel. Capital One also provides access to travel redemptions and participating transfer partners. Depending on the current program, miles can potentially be used toward eligible travel purchases or transferred into participating airline and hotel loyalty programs. For both ecosystems, transfer partners create opportunities, but also introduce complexity. Award availability can disappear. Airlines can change award pricing. Taxes and surcharges can be substantial, and transferring points into an airline program is generally not something you should do without a specific redemption strategy. Once transferable points have been moved into an external loyalty program, reversing that transfer may not be possible. For executive travel, the strongest strategy is often to search for the flight first, determine the cash price, determine the award price, calculate the effective value per point, then transfer only the points required for the booking. There is another issue that high-spending businesses should not ignore. Operational resilience. If millions of dollars in annual expenses are being routed through one card ecosystem, a temporary fraud review, transaction decline, account restriction, or payment processing problem could disrupt company operations. A sophisticated corporate card strategy, therefore, should not depend entirely on a single payment instrument. Businesses with substantial operating expenses may benefit from maintaining multiple payment methods and allocating spending according to the strengths of each. That can also change the Venture X Business versus Business Platinum question. For some companies, the correct answer may not be choosing one and eliminating the other. It may be using each card selectively. A flat-rate card can handle eligible general operating expenses. Another card can be used when its category bonuses, travel benefits, purchasing capacity, or redemption features create greater value. But, rewards should remain secondary to financial controls. Your accounting team needs clean reconciliation. Employee cards need appropriate controls. Fraud monitoring needs to be effective. Cash must be available when payments are due. And card usage should integrate cleanly with the company's expense management and accounting systems. A 2% rewards difference means very little if poor treasury management creates interest, late fees, cash flow problems, or accounting complexity. So, which card is better? The Capital One Venture X Business can be compelling for businesses that prioritize a straightforward earning structure on broad eligible spending and value the Capital One travel ecosystem. The American Express Business Platinum can be compelling for companies that can extract meaningful value from its current bonus categories, premium travel benefits, purchasing flexibility, and membership rewards ecosystem. But, neither [clears throat] card is automatically superior for every high-spending company. Before applying, take your previous 12 months of business transactions and model them against the current earning rules, annual fees, credits, payment requirements, and redemption options of both cards. Then, calculate the expected net value after fees. That is the number that matters, not the headline multiplier, not the size of the welcome bonus, and not the theoretical value of millions of points you may never redeem efficiently. Which business card ecosystem does your company currently use for major operating expenses? metadata.title: HOW TO PREPARE FOR A TICKETMASTER VERIFIED FAN PRESALE | BUY PRESALE TICKETS WAITLISTED VS SELECTED
metadata.author: thumbsuprun
metadata.shortDescription:
The Ticketmaster Verified Fan Presale is already difficult enough to understand as it is, but what happens after you've submitted your request? Well, there are only two outcomes: waitlist or selected. Which one are you and what's the difference?

00:00 // Introduction
1:29 // What It Means If You're Waitlisted on Ticketmaster
4:23 // You've Been Selected! How To Prepare For Ticketmaster Verified Fan Presale
8:04 // Morning Of Presale - What To Do
10:18 // What Device Should You Use For Verified Fan Presales?

If you're waitlisted, then you won't be able to participate in the Ticketmaster Verified Fan Presale when it first goes on sale, simple as that. You may eventually receive a code later in the day but I wouldn't count on it. You may be feeling down and depressed based on the outcome but don't just buy tickets on the open market just yet...you still got a chance on the general sale! Gather yourself together and try again then before forcing yourself to buy tickets from resale ticket marketplaces!

If you've been selected....congrats! You are a true fan in the eyes of Ticketmaster! Lots of amazing and wonderful things are about to come your way, including being able to buy some great seats at even better prices. However, you do need to spend a bit of time preparing before you can simply jump into the queue and buy your seats.

Before anything else, make sure you find your code and specific event URL from your mobile device and keep that set aside. Do not lose this as they won't send it again! As you review this information, you'll be able to confirm your city and date of the event you registered for as the URL will take you to the exact event you'll be purchasing tickets for. 

Next up is to remember to set an alarm for the event itself. I cannot tell you how many times I have missed a presale because I simply...wasn't paying attention. It's so easy to get distracted or tell yourself you'll get back to something later, only to forget about it completely. After that, take some time to review the seating chart and get a good idea of where you'd like to sit. Give yourself a few options though because depending on your placement in the queue, you may end up at the front, middle, or end, it's all luck of the draw. 

After a good night's rest, be sure to jump into the queue about 10-15 minutes before it opens. You can technically join the queue as soon as it is available but I prefer to wait closer to event time because again, may forget about it otherwise. Remember that you can only join the queue with the account that registered for the show, so if you try to log into the wrong account, it will give you an error and turn you away. 

Also, try not to wait until the final second to join the queue as you may still need to go through a two-factor authentication to confirm your identity. You'll need your phone nearby so don't forget!

Speaking of phones, it may be best to actually access the presale from your computer or laptop instead of a mobile device as the Ticketmaster Verified Fan Presale was originally designed for a computer experience. If you only have a mobile option, go ahead and use that, but if you can, I would certainly recommend using a computer if available. 

Last thing I want to mention, do NOT try to log into the queue multiple times. This will create issues and cause you to lose your original spot and potentially stop you from being able to access the presale at all. It isn't worth it as there is 0 upside. None. Don't do it.

After all that, just keep your code on copy/paste, and once you get through the queue, simply paste your presale code into the box and you're ready to go ahead and purchase those amazing seats and have all the fun! 

Let me know in the comments below if you have any other questions related to the Ticketmaster Verified Fan Presale process!
